Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] OpenClaw paste-site (rentry.co/glot.io) curl-pipe-bash semantic-hijack dropper · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] cluw macOS stealer shell dropper fetching payload from ClawHavoc/AMOS C2 IP · [LLM] cluw infostealer and malicious ClawHub skill payload hashes on macOS · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress to ClawHavoc cluw / AMOS C2 infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
cluw macOS stealer shell dropper fetching payload from ClawHavoc/AMOS C2 IP AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OpenClaw-skill prerequisite-block dropper: a macOS shell process (curl/bash/base64) whose command line references the cluw C2 at 2.26.75.16, the payload path /Xuvewuyur, or the persistent AMOS C2 at 91.92.242.30. This is the exact curl-pipe-bash delivery Unit 42 attributed to the tradingview-ai-indicator-assistant skill. Rationale: Pins on three hard article IOCs (cluw C2 2.26.75.16, payload path /Xuvewuyur, AMOS C2 91.92.242.30) in shell command lines — the literal curl-pipe-bash prerequisite-block delivery. 91.92.242.30 cross-confirmed by ThreatFox + Trend Micro; 2.26.75.16//Xuvewuyur are Unit 42-original. Cross-checked against: • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/malware/osx.amos/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/b/openclaw-skills-used-to-distribute-atomic-macos-stealer.html • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the tradingview-ai-indicator-assistant skill in a sandbox VM
  • Threat-intel team curling the C2 to capture the payload for analysis
  • Internal IR replay of the IOC during a tabletop exercise
  • Network-range coincidence: an unrelated internal host legitimately assigned 2.26.75.16 in a lab (verify it is the public C2, not RFC1918)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vmware-tools","sandbox-agent") and DeviceName !startswith "MALWARE-LAB"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the matching process is on a macOS endpoint with OpenClaw installed; pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain — the parent should be the OpenClaw agent/terminal, not a sandbox tool. 2) CONTAIN: Network-isolate the host, block 2.26.75.16 + 91.92.242.30 + the /Xuvewuyur URL at egress, and treat all credentials/API keys/keychain secrets reachable by the agent as compromised — force rotation. 3) HUNT: Search the same host and all OpenClaw users for the cluw hash (818aea61...), installed ClawHub skills published by the banned accounts, and any cron/LaunchAgent persistence pointing at the C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("2.26.75.16", "91.92.242.30", "/Xuvewuyur")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","bash","sh","zsh","base64","python","python3","osascript")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("2.26.75.16", "91.92.242.30", "/Xuvewuyur")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("curl","wget","bash","base64","sh","python")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network egress to ClawHavoc cluw / AMOS C2 infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any outbound connection to the cluw C2 (2.26.75.16) or the still-active AMOS dropper C2 (91.92.242.30) that distributes payloads via malicious OpenClaw/ClawHub skills. Pure IOC match independent of the delivery binary, so it catches second-stage beaconing the process-tree query may miss. Rationale: Direct match on the two campaign C2 IPs. 91.92.242.30 is corroborated as live AMOS infra by ThreatFox and Trend Micro three months after first disclosure; 2.26.75.16 is the newly-discovered cluw C2 from Unit 42 — any internal host reaching either is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/malware/osx.amos/ • https://www.koi.ai/blog/clawhavoc-341-malicious-clawedbot-skills-found-by-the-bot-they-were-targeting • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel proxy or TI-platform sandbox actively polling the C2
  • Security scanner / ASM tooling fingerprinting the IP range
  • Lab VM detonating the cluw sample with live network
  • An internal asset coincidentally NATed behind a proxy that re-uses 2.26.75.16 as a public egress (verify ownership)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ti-sandbox","threatconnect-collector")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a shell/curl or the OpenClaw agent is malicious; a TI sandbox is benign. Confirm direction is outbound to the public C2. 2) CONTAIN: Block both IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and snapshot for forensics. Rotate any secrets the OpenClaw agent could reach (keychain, API tokens, SSH keys). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the host for the cluw dropper command line, the 818aea61... hash, ClawHub skill installs, and cron/LaunchAgent persistence re-establishing the channel.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("2.26.75.16", "91.92.242.30")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("2.26.75.16", "91.92.242.30")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

cluw infostealer and malicious ClawHub skill payload hashes on macOS AIInstallation Medium
Alerts when any of the Unit 42 / Trend Micro file hashes for the malicious ClawHub skills or the cluw macOS infostealer are written or executed. Catches the payload regardless of which paste-site or C2 delivered it. Rationale: Exact-hash IOC sweep for the skill package (b6c7e0bf...) and cluw stealer (818aea61...) plus the four additional ClawHub skill hashes from the IOC set. Hashes are zero-FP by nature; the skill SHA256 is in both Unit 42 and Trend Micro's bundle. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/content/dam/trendmicro/global/en/research/26/b/amos-stealer-openclaw/ioc-malicious-openclaw-skills-used-to-distribute-atomic-macos-stealer.txt • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR quarantine copy of the sample retaining the original hash on a security-team workstation
  • Malware repository / VirusTotal mirror stored on an internal research host
  • Backup or DLP system snapshotting a host that already held the payload
  • Purple-team retaining the sample for detection-engineering tests
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !contains "/Malware/" and DeviceName !startswith "SEC-RESEARCH"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the hash landed on a production macOS endpoint (not a malware-analysis host) and check FileOriginUrl/parent for the rentry.co or C2 source. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, quarantine the file, and rotate every secret the OpenClaw agent could access — keychain, API keys, SSH keys, crypto wallet keys. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all ClawHub skills installed by the user, look for Telegram Bot API exfil and cron/LaunchAgent persistence, and sweep the fleet for the same hashes and the C2 IPs.

OpenClaw paste-site (rentry.co/glot.io) curl-pipe-bash semantic-hijack dropper AIDelivery Medium
Hunting query for the ClawHavoc prerequisite-block lure pattern: a shell command line that fetches from a paste-site redirect (rentry.co/openclaw-code, glot.io) and pipes a Base64-decoded payload to a shell. Catches new variants that rotate C2 IPs but reuse the paste-site delivery, including the copy-paste-into-terminal lure. Rationale: Targets the durable behavioural pattern Unit 42, Koi and Trend Micro all describe (paste-site redirect lure + Base64-pipe-to-bash) rather than a single rotating IP, with the article-specific rentry.co/openclaw-code path as the high-fidelity anchor. Hunting tier because legit dev tooling also uses curl|bash one-liners. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/clawhavoc-341-malicious-clawedbot-skills-found-by-the-bot-they-were-targeting • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/b/openclaw-skills-used-to-distribute-atomic-macos-stealer.html • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer installing a CLI tool via a documented rentry.co/glot.io curl|bash one-liner
  • CI/CD bootstrap script pulling a config snippet from glot.io
  • Homebrew/oh-my-zsh style install one-liners that pipe curl to bash (different domain but same shape if allowlist too broad)
  • Security-team replay of the lure during awareness training
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("brew","git") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("githubusercontent.com","brew.sh"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full command line — confirm the fetched paste-site is rentry.co/openclaw-code or another OpenClaw-themed slug, and that the parent is the OpenClaw agent or a terminal driven by it. Decode any inline Base64 to reveal the downstream URL/C2. 2) CONTAIN: If the decoded payload hits 2.26.75.16/91.92.242.30 or drops the cluw hash, isolate the host, block the paste-site path and C2, and rotate agent-reachable secrets. 3) HUNT: Inventory installed ClawHub skills for fake 'Prerequisites' blocks, and sweep for cron/LaunchAgent auto-updater persistence and Telegram Bot API exfil.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rentry.co/openclaw-code", "rentry.co", "glot.io")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64", "| bash", "|bash", "| sh", "| zsh", "curl -", "-fsSL")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("rentry.co/openclaw-code", "rentry.co", "glot.io")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("base64", "bash", "curl", "| sh")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"

| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")

   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d") or SHA1 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d") or MD5 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d") or SHA1 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d") or MD5 in~ ("b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b6c7e0bf573b1c7d9d3a05eb08d26579199515b847df984862805f44a7af8007", "818aea6143282b352fdfdc0f3ebf77a36e54eb3befb5cad1a355a99ab97c6aa7", "b30eaed1f7478c28f4ec50d07ed5ef014ffbc4b2bc5a38d689ba9f7abb5e19c2", "ebb73dbb5aac1f6fe1a88e8f26126a1e1aa34c9f3345ad4345189b40d9bf1d1d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS.Gaslight Telegram Bot API C2 polling from non-browser process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts macOS endpoints resolving/connecting to api.telegram.org from a process that is not a known browser or the legitimate Telegram desktop client. macOS.Gaslight runs its C2 as a Telegram Bot API getUpdates polling loop, so sustained api.telegram.org traffic from an ad-hoc-signed Rust binary is the C2 fingerprint. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim getUpdates Telegram Bot API C2 (code block 2) plus the api.telegram.org endpoint; non-browser/non-Telegram initiating process is the differentiator. Cross-checked against SentinelLABS, Infosecurity Magazine and the PXA/Ghost-in-the-Zip Telegram-C2 reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/macos-gaslight-rust-backdoor/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/ghost-in-the-zip-new-pxa-stealer-and-its-telegram-powered-ecosystem/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Telegram Desktop client installed under a non-standard process name
  • Developer/CI tooling using a Telegram bot for build notifications
  • Marketing or alerting scripts (python/node) posting to a Telegram bot
  • Browser extensions or Electron apps embedding Telegram web
  • Security tooling that itself proxies Telegram traffic
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/Applications/Telegram.app"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 and folder path; confirm it is not Telegram Desktop or a sanctioned bot integration, and check if the binary is ad-hoc signed in an unusual path (e.g. user temp/Application Support). 2) Contain: isolate the host in MDE/Falcon, kill the polling process, and block the resolved IPs at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SHA256/parent across the fleet, and look for login.keychain-db copies, collected_data.zip, and the com.apple.system.services.activity LaunchAgent on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Telegram","Telegram.app","Safari","com.apple.Safari","Google Chrome","Google Chrome Helper","firefox","Brave Browser","com.apple.WebKit.Networking","nsurlsessiond")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), DistinctMinutes=dcount(bin(Timestamp,1m)) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteUrl
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has "api.telegram.org"
| summarize Lookups=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

macOS.Gaslight keychain theft + collected_data.zip staging AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the macOS.Gaslight Python stealer copying login.keychain-db and archiving harvested data to collected_data.zip prior to Telegram exfiltration. The collected_data.zip filename and a login.keychain-db copy by a non-Apple process are high-fidelity collection indicators. Rationale: Uses the article's exact collection artifacts: a raw copy of login.keychain-db and the temp/collected_data.zip archive. SentinelLABS notes AMOS/early Rust macOS stealers harvest the same login.keychain-db, and Jamf documents DumpKeychain()-style theft, so the zip filename is the novel high-fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/pyinstaller-malware-jamf-threat-labs/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/02/infostealers-without-borders-macos-python-stealers-and-platform-abuse/
ATT&CKT1555.001 T1560.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Time Machine / backupd legitimately reading login.keychain-db
  • Keychain First Aid or migration assistant copying the keychain during OS upgrade
  • Admin manually backing up ~/Library/Keychains before re-imaging
  • A user-created archive coincidentally named collected_data.zip (rare)
  • MDM agents snapshotting user profiles
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "login.keychain-db" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("backupd","securityd","Migration Assistant"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess copying login.keychain-db / writing collected_data.zip — legitimate copies come from backupd/securityd, not a user-temp binary. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, and force-rotate any credentials/secrets stored in that user's keychain (SSO, VPN, cloud, SSH passphrases). 3) Hunt: look for the collected_data.zip being uploaded to api.telegram.org, the com.apple.system.services.activity LaunchAgent, and the same parent binary's SHA256 elsewhere.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName =~ "collected_data.zip")
    or (FileName =~ "login.keychain-db" and ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backupd","mds","mds_stores","securityd","TimeMachine","cfprefsd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "collected_data.zip")
    or (TargetFileName =~ "login.keychain-db" and EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed"))
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("backupd","mds","mds_stores","securityd","cfprefsd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS.Gaslight LaunchAgent persistence masquerading as com.apple.system.services.activity AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist using the macOS.Gaslight persistence label com.apple.system.services.activity, an Apple-lookalike name not used by any genuine Apple service. Catches the implant establishing a persistent foothold. Rationale: Anchored on the exact LaunchAgent Label IOC from Table 2 (com.apple.system.services.activity) — there is no genuine Apple LaunchAgent by that name, so any plist bearing it is the implant. Consistent with SentinelLABS BlueNoroff/RustBucket macOS LaunchAgent persistence tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/bluenoroff-hidden-risk-threat-actor-targets-macs-with-fake-crypto-news-and-novel-persistence/
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Apple LaunchAgents (com.apple.*) — but none use the exact services.activity suffix
  • Internal MDM/config-profile deployment pushing a custom-labeled agent (would not impersonate com.apple.*)
  • Security product creating its own LaunchDaemon under a vendor label
  • Developer testing a self-named LaunchAgent during app packaging
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the plist contents (ProgramArguments) and the InitiatingProcess that wrote it; confirm the referenced binary path and signing status. 2) Contain: unload the agent (launchctl bootout), quarantine the referenced binary, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to the binary's SHA256 across the fleet and check for api.telegram.org C2, login.keychain-db copies, and IOPMAssertionCreateWithName no-sleep behavior on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" or FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchDaemons/"
| where FileName has "com.apple.system.services.activity"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" or TargetFilePath has "/Library/LaunchDaemons/"
| where TargetFileName has "com.apple.system.services.activity"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS.Gaslight self-staged standalone CPython 3.10.18 fetch (astral-sh python-build-standalone) AIInstallation High
Detects the macOS.Gaslight bash installer fetching a self-contained cpython-3.10.18 (build 20250708) interpreter from astral-sh/python-build-standalone at runtime — a novel staging step that precedes the Python keychain stealer. Anchors on the literal PY_VERSION/BUILD_DATE constants and the project name in the command line. Rationale: Uses the verbatim installer constants PY_VERSION=3.10.18 and BUILD_DATE=20250708 plus the astral-sh/python-build-standalone project name. SentinelLABS and Microsoft both flag runtime CPython staging as a novel macOS stealer delivery, making these literals high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/astral-sh/python-build-standalone • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/02/infostealers-without-borders-macos-python-stealers-and-platform-abuse/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer using uv/rye/astral tooling that downloads python-build-standalone
  • CI runner provisioning a standalone CPython for build reproducibility
  • Data-science user manually fetching a portable CPython 3.10.18
  • Package manager (e.g. uv) auto-installing the same interpreter version
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("uv","rye","pyenv","brew")
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the full command line and parent process — a developer fetch comes from uv/rye/terminal; the implant fetch is spawned by a base64-decoded bash installer with emoji/AI-comment tells. 2) Contain: if the parent is not a sanctioned dev tool, isolate host, kill the bash/curl chain, quarantine the staged interpreter dir. 3) Hunt: look for the subsequent Python process touching login.keychain-db, system_profiler, ps aux, and creating collected_data.zip, plus api.telegram.org egress.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "python-build-standalone"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "astral-sh" and ProcessCommandLine has "cpython-3.10.18")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "PY_VERSION=3.10.18" and ProcessCommandLine has "BUILD_DATE=20250708")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "python-build-standalone"
    or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "astral-sh" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "cpython-3.10.18")
    or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "PY_VERSION=3.10.18" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "BUILD_DATE=20250708")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS.Gaslight known-bad file hashes (Mach-O implant, BONZAI sibling, Python/bash stages) AIInstallation Medium
Direct IOC sweep for the four published macOS.Gaslight SHA256 hashes and the ad-hoc signing SHA1, covering the Rust Mach-O implant, the sibling BONZAI sample, the base64 Python stealer, and the bash CPython installer. Fires on execution or file write of any known artifact. Rationale: Direct sweep on the four article SHA256 IOCs (Table 2) plus the ad-hoc signing SHA1 5555494492fc..., covering all four stage artifacts. Hash-only detections are deterministic; XProtect tracks the same sample by hash under MACOS_BONZAI_COBUCH. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/macos-gaslight-rust-backdoor-turns-prompt-injection-on-the-analyst-not-the-sandbox/ • https://cyberpress.org/gaslight-backdoor-misleads-analysts/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hash collision is cryptographically implausible — effectively zero benign matches
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned analysis VM
  • Threat-intel platform re-scanning the artifact during enrichment
  • EDR's own quarantine/restore re-touching the file (Evidence=File)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the matched hash and host; any non-sandbox match is a confirmed compromise — record device, user, folder path. 2) Contain: isolate host immediately, quarantine the file, and revoke credentials/keychain secrets for the logged-on user. 3) Hunt: pivot to api.telegram.org C2, the com.apple.system.services.activity LaunchAgent, login.keychain-db copies, and collected_data.zip; sweep the fleet for all four hashes and the ad-hoc signing identifier endpoint-macos-aarch64.
let GaslightHashes = dynamic(["6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525","77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca","baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239","b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394"]);
let GaslightSha1 = "5555494492fc075f441637fb9d894913dde3a2ea";
union
( DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in~ (GaslightHashes) or SHA1 =~ GaslightSha1 | extend Evidence="Process" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Evidence, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in~ (GaslightHashes) or SHA1 =~ GaslightSha1 | extend Evidence="File", ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Evidence, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine )
| order by Timestamp desc
let GaslightHashes = dynamic(["6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525","77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca","baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239","b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394"]);
union
( ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in~ (GaslightHashes) | extend Evidence="Process" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, Evidence, TargetProcessName, SHA256, TargetProcessCommandLine ),
( ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (GaslightHashes) | extend Evidence="File", SHA256=TargetFileSHA256, TargetProcessName=ActingProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, Evidence, TargetProcessName, SHA256, TargetProcessCommandLine )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"

        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394") or SHA1 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394") or MD5 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394") or SHA1 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394") or MD5 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-06-23 6 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A forgotten credential at vendor Klue let attackers reach customers' Salesforce data. How modern SaaS breaches cascade, and the keys you should audit.

IPs138.226.246.94 212.86.125.24 213.111.148.90 94.154.32.160

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Salesforce connected-app OAuth access from first-seen ISP / anonymizing proxy (stolen-token reuse) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Klue/Icarus: bulk Salesforce CRM record retrieval via connected app (Case/Contact/Account/Opportunity) · [LLM] Salesforce API access bearing python-requests/aiohttp automation user-agent (Icarus OAuth abuse) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Klue/Icarus: bulk Salesforce CRM record retrieval via connected app (Case/Contact/Account/Opportunity) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the high-volume automated read/export of Salesforce CRM objects performed by the compromised Klue OAuth integration during the June 2026 Icarus/UNC6395 campaign. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact CRM objects (Case, Contact, Account, Opportunity) that were mass-queried via SOQL/bulk export by an authorized third-party connected app rather than an interactive user. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CRM objects (Case/Contact/Account/Opportunity) that Mandiant/Google Cloud confirmed were bulk-SOQL-queried and exported by the abused OAuth connected app, plus a per-hour volume threshold that separates a productized SaaS connector's steady sync from an attacker's automated mass extraction. Cross-checked against: • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4187907/klue-breach-exposed-salesforce-crm-data-through-stolen-oauth-tokens.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoftthreatprotectionblog/protect-against-oauth-attacks-in-salesforce-with-microsoft-defender/4450584
ATT&CKT1119 T1213 T1567.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Nightly/scheduled Klue competitive-intel sync legitimately reading Account/Opportunity records
  • Sales-ops bulk report exports or Salesforce Data Loader jobs run by admins
  • Data-warehouse ETL connectors (Fivetran, Informatica, Mulesoft) extracting CRM objects on a schedule
  • SaaS backup tooling (OwnBackup/Own, Spanning) performing full-object snapshots
  • Marketing/RevOps enrichment integrations doing periodic full-table pulls
Suppression filter
| where AccountObjectId !in ("<known-klue-integration-objectid-AFTER-revalidation>") and not (UserAgents has_any ("Salesforce Data Loader","OwnBackup","Fivetran","Informatica"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the AccountObjectId/CONNECTED_APP_NAME driving the spike — confirm whether it is the Klue integration service account and compare the hour's RecordOps to the prior 30-day baseline for that identity. Pull the UserAgents and SrcIPs aggregated. 2) CONTAIN: If it is Klue (or any unexpected connected app) exceeding baseline, disable/revoke the connected app's OAuth authorization in Salesforce Setup > Connected Apps OAuth Usage and revoke its tokens; do not just block the IP. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same AccountObjectId across all Salesforce ActionTypes for the last 14 days, look for python-requests/aiohttp user-agents (UC2) and first-seen source ISPs (UC3), and enumerate exactly which records were read for breach-notification scoping.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Api","ReportExport","Report exported","Bulk","Mass","Export","Read")
| where ObjectType in~ ("Case","Contact","Account","Opportunity") or isempty(ObjectType)
| summarize RecordOps = count(),
            DistinctRecords = dcount(ObjectId),
            ObjectsTouched = make_set(ObjectType, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 10),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 15),

            by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountType, ApplicationId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where RecordOps > 1000   // bulk automated pull; productized Klue sync runs far lower, attacker mass-export spikes
| order by RecordOps desc

sourcetype="sfdc:reportexport" OR sourcetype="sfdc:api" OR sourcetype="sfdc:restapi" OR sourcetype="sfdc:bulkapi"

Salesforce API access bearing python-requests/aiohttp automation user-agent (Icarus OAuth abuse) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Salesforce API/bulk calls whose user-agent is a raw Python HTTP library (python-requests, aiohttp), which Mandiant attributed to the Icarus/UNC6395 exfiltration scripts in the Klue/Salesloft-Drift OAuth campaign. Article-specific because a productized SaaS connector like Klue does not present python-requests/aiohttp as its session user-agent — that fingerprint indicates the stolen token is being driven by an attacker's ad-hoc script. Rationale: The python-requests/aiohttp user-agent is a high-fidelity, second-source-confirmed (Mandiant/Google Cloud) fingerprint of the Icarus exfil scripts driving a stolen OAuth token, and it cleanly distinguishes scripted attacker access from a legitimate productized connector's normal session UA. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://www.rescana.com/post/salesloft-drift-oauth-token-breach-enables-salesforce-data-theft-in-unc6395-icarus-attack-campaign-august-2026
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004 T1071.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • In-house Python integration scripts legitimately calling the Salesforce REST/Bulk API with a default user-agent
  • CI/CD jobs or scheduled data pipelines built on requests/aiohttp pulling CRM data
  • QA/sandbox automation against a production org
  • A developer running an ad-hoc simple_salesforce/requests script for a one-off pull
  • Low-code/iPaaS connector that happens to surface a python-requests UA
Suppression filter
| where AccountObjectId !in ("<known-internal-python-integration-objectid>") and AccountType != "DeveloperSandbox"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine which AccountObjectId/CONNECTED_APP the python-requests/aiohttp sessions authenticated as — if it is an OAuth connected-app/service identity (not a named developer), treat as high priority and pull the SrcIPs and Objects accessed. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the connected app's OAuth tokens and disable the integration in Salesforce; rotate the integration credential/secret. 3) HUNT: Correlate the same SrcIPs/AccountObjectId against UC1 (bulk record volume) and UC3 (new source infra); if confirmed, enumerate every object/record touched by those sessions for notification scope and check for log-tampering (Setup Audit Trail gaps).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where UserAgent has_any ("python-requests","aiohttp","python-urllib","Python/3")
| summarize EventCount = count(),
            Actions = make_set(ActionType, 12),
            Objects = make_set(ObjectType, 12),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 15),
            ISPs = make_set(ISP, 8),
            AnonProxy = make_set(IsAnonymousProxy, 3)
            by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountType, UserAgent
| order by EventCount desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where UserAgent has_any ("python-requests","aiohttp","python-urllib","Python/3")
| summarize EventCount = count(),
            Actions = make_set(ActionType, 12),
            Objects = make_set(ObjectType, 12),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 15),
            ISPs = make_set(ISP, 8),
            AnonProxy = make_set(IsAnonymousProxy, 3)
            by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountType, UserAgent
| order by EventCount desc
WEB
sourcetype="sfdc:api" OR sourcetype="sfdc:restapi" OR sourcetype="sfdc:bulkapi" OR sourcetype="sfdc:reportexport"
| where like(lower(USER_AGENT),"%python-requests%") OR like(lower(USER_AGENT),"%aiohttp%") OR like(lower(USER_AGENT),"%python-urllib%")
| stats count AS Hits values(EVENT_TYPE) AS EventTypes values(ENTITY_NAME) AS Objects dc(CLIENT_IP) AS SrcIPCount values(CLIENT_IP) AS SrcIPs min(_time) AS firstSeen max(_time) AS lastSeen by USER_NAME, USER_ID, USER_AGENT, CONNECTED_APP_NAME
| sort - Hits
Salesforce connected-app OAuth access from first-seen ISP / anonymizing proxy (stolen-token reuse) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces Salesforce activity for a connected-app/service identity arriving from a source ISP never previously associated with that identity, or flagged as an anonymizing proxy — the signature of an attacker replaying a harvested OAuth token from their own infrastructure rather than from Klue's. Article-specific because the breach hinged on a long-lived integration token being used from attacker-controlled (proxied) infrastructure. Rationale: Replays the core breach mechanic — a long-lived OAuth/service token used from new (often anonymized) infrastructure — by leftanti-joining today's Salesforce source ISPs per identity against a 30-day baseline and prioritizing anonymous-proxy hits, which catches token theft even when API calls themselves look legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4187907/klue-breach-exposed-salesforce-crm-data-through-stolen-oauth-tokens.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1528 T1090.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Klue (or another connected app) legitimately changing its egress IP/ISP after a cloud-provider migration or scaling event
  • A traveling admin or service account routed through a new corporate VPN/egress point
  • Genuine new integration deployed in the last 24h presenting a never-before-seen ISP
  • Cloud-hosted ETL/backup tooling whose provider rotates outbound IP ranges
  • Identity using a privacy-VPN endpoint flagged as anonymous proxy but operated by an employee
Suppression filter
| where not (ISP in ("<known-klue-egress-isp>","<corp-vpn-isp>") and AnyAnonProxy == false)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each first-seen ISP/identity pair, confirm whether the AccountObjectId is a connected-app/service identity and whether the new ISP/anon-proxy is expected (check change tickets for new integrations or vendor IP changes). 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained — especially anonymous-proxy hits on the Klue integration identity — revoke the connected app's OAuth tokens, force token re-issuance, and rotate the integration secret. 3) HUNT: Join this identity+IP back to UC1 (bulk reads) and UC2 (python UAs) within the same window; if any correlate, scope all records accessed from those sessions and review the Setup Audit Trail for evidence of log clearing.
let Lookback = 30d;
let Baseline = CloudAppEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(1d))
    | where Application == "Salesforce"
    | summarize by AccountObjectId, ISP;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where isnotempty(AccountObjectId)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountObjectId, ISP
| summarize EventCount = count(),
            Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10),
            Objects = make_set(ObjectType, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 8),
            AnyAnonProxy = max(tobool(IsAnonymousProxy))
            by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountType, IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode
| order by AnyAnonProxy desc, FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let Lookback = 30d;
let Baseline = CloudAppEvents
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(1d))
    | where Application == "Salesforce"
    | summarize by AccountObjectId, ISP;
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where isnotempty(AccountObjectId)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountObjectId, ISP
| summarize EventCount = count(),
            Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10),
            Objects = make_set(ObjectType, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 8),
            AnyAnonProxy = max(tobool(IsAnonymousProxy))
            by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, AccountType, IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode
| order by AnyAnonProxy desc, FirstSeen desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) AS firstSeen max(_time) AS lastSeen from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="Salesforce" earliest=-1d by Authentication.user, Authentication.src, Authentication.app

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="Salesforce" earliest=-30d latest=-1d by Authentication.user, Authentication.src
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents

The Global Namespace Risk: Universal Bucket Hijacking Technique for Cloud Data Exfiltration

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-22 6 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Unit 42 research details how attackers could exploit global name uniqueness in bucket hijacking to redirect cloud data streams across major CSPs. The post The Global Namespace Risk: Universal Bucket Hijacking Technique for Cloud Data Exfiltration appeared first on Unit 42 .

ATT&CKT1190 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Reconnaissance

—

Exploitation
Detected

Detected

Likely
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GCS bucket deletion of a logging-sink / data-stream destination (bucket-hijack precursor) · [LLM] AWS S3 DeleteBucket on a replication / log-delivery destination (bucket-hijack precursor) · [LLM] AWS S3 bucket DeleteBucket then CreateBucket of the SAME name across accounts (hijack signature)
GCS bucket deletion of a logging-sink / data-stream destination (bucket-hijack precursor) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts deletion of a Google Cloud Storage bucket via storage.buckets.delete - the pivotal step in the Unit 42 universal bucket-hijacking technique, where an attacker deletes a sink/Pub-Sub/Storage-Transfer destination bucket so they can recreate the globally-unique name in their own project and reroute the data stream. Article-specific because it keys on the exact GCP IAM method named in the research rather than generic storage activity. Rationale: Keys on the exact GCP method storage.buckets.delete (and the storage.objects.delete empty-step) named in the Unit 42 research as the required hijack permissions; the bucket-delete is the only victim-side-visible event in the technique. Cross-checked Unit 42 article and MITRE T1537. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cloud-bucket-hijacking-risks/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1537/
ATT&CKT1485 T1537
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned decommissioning of a project / log archive bucket by a platform engineer
  • Terraform/Deployment-Manager teardown of ephemeral environments deleting and recreating buckets
  • CI/CD pipeline that rotates test buckets each run
  • Lifecycle automation emptying then deleting expired buckets
  • Org migration consolidating storage into a new bucket name
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the deleted bucket name and confirm whether it was a destination for a logging sink, Pub/Sub subscription, or Storage Transfer job (it should NOT have been deleted while still referenced). Check the principalEmail and callerIp against known platform-admin identities/CI service accounts. 2) Contain: if the deletion was unexpected, freeze the actor's credentials/key and immediately re-create the bucket name in YOUR project to deny the attacker the global namespace claim; verify the sink is still writing to your project. 3) Hunt: search for the same bucket name being created in any external/unfamiliar project, prior storage.objects.delete bursts on that bucket, and the IAM grants (logging.sinks.update, storage roles) that preceded the delete.
