| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(protoPayload.resourceName) as bucket values(protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp) as src_ip by protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail, resource.labels.project_id
| sort - lastTime
AWS S3 DeleteBucket on a replication / log-delivery destination (bucket-hijack precursor) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CloudTrail DeleteBucket on S3 - the destructive step that lets an attacker re-register the globally-unique bucket name in their own account and silently reroute an S3 replication or log-delivery stream per the Unit 42 technique. Deliberately distinct from the existing PutBucketReplication detection: it pivots on the delete, not the replication-config change. Rationale: Pivots on the CloudTrail DeleteBucket API named in the Unit 42 technique as the destructive precursor to recreating a hijacked globally-unique name; intentionally avoids overlap with Splunk's existing PutBucketReplication rule. Corroborated by MITRE T1537 and Splunk Security Content's bucket-replication exfil detection. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cloud-bucket-hijacking-risks/ • https://research.splunk.com/cloud/eeb432d6-2212-43b6-9e89-fcd753f7da4c/ • https://www.varonis.com/blog/preventing-s3-bucket-namesquatting
ATT&CKT1485 T1537
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineer decommissioning a stale data-lake or log-archive bucket
  • Terraform/CloudFormation stack deletion tearing down a bucket
  • CI/CD ephemeral-bucket cleanup at end of build
  • Cost-optimization sweep removing empty/unused buckets
  • Account closure / region migration consolidating storage
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the deleted bucket was an active replication destination or log-delivery target (CloudTrail/S3 server access / ELB / Config delivery). Check the caller ARN, sourceIPAddress and userAgent against approved IaC pipelines. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, immediately recreate the bucket name in the legitimate account to reclaim the global namespace, apply a restrictive bucket policy, and revoke the actor's session/keys. Enforce a data-perimeter SCP blocking writes to external-account buckets. 3) Hunt: look for PutBucketReplication or PutBucketLogging pointing the source at this name, GetBucketReplication recon, and any CreateBucket of the same name in another account.
title: AWS S3 Bucket Deletion (Bucket Hijacking Precursor)
id: 1d83b6f2-5a47-4c19-bb20-9f4e1c7a6d52
description: Detects S3 DeleteBucket events that may precede a globally-unique-name bucket hijack used to reroute replication or log-delivery streams.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cloud-bucket-hijacking-risks/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:
  - attack.t1485
  - attack.t1537
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventSource: s3.amazonaws.com
    eventName: DeleteBucket
  filter_err:
    errorCode: '*'
  condition: selection and not filter_err
level: medium
source:cloudtrail @eventSource:s3.amazonaws.com @evt.name:DeleteBucket @evt.outcome:success
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, userAgent, requestParameters.bucketName, awsRegion
| filter eventSource = "s3.amazonaws.com" and eventName = "DeleteBucket" and not isPresent(errorCode)
| sort @timestamp desc
CLOUD
sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource="s3.amazonaws.com" eventName=DeleteBucket
| search NOT errorCode=*
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(sourceIPAddress) as src_ip values(userAgent) as user_agent by requestParameters.bucketName, userIdentity.arn, awsRegion, recipientAccountId
| sort - lastTime
AWS S3 bucket DeleteBucket then CreateBucket of the SAME name across accounts (hijack signature) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates an S3 DeleteBucket immediately followed by a CreateBucket of the identical bucket name in a different account within an organization CloudTrail - the exact delete-and-recreate-under-attacker-account sequence Unit 42 describes. High-fidelity because legitimate workflows almost never delete a bucket in one account and recreate the same globally-unique name in another. Rationale: Encodes the literal hijack signature from the Unit 42 article - delete the bucket, then recreate the same globally-unique name under a different (attacker) account - as a cross-account temporal correlation on bucketName, which is far higher fidelity than either event alone. Validated against MITRE T1537 (same-provider account-to-account transfer). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cloud-bucket-hijacking-risks/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1537/
ATT&CKT1537 T1485
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned cross-account migration moving a bucket to a new account under the same org
  • Disaster-recovery rehearsal recreating a bucket name in a backup account
  • Account-vending pipeline that recreates standardized bucket names per account
  • Manual admin recreating a mistakenly-deleted bucket in a different account
  • Blue-team validation of this exact namespace-reclaim mitigation
Suppression filter
| where NOT match(requestParameters.bucketName, "^(tmp|test|ci|build|ephemeral)-")
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the recipientAccountId of the DeleteBucket vs the CreateBucket - if the recreating account is outside your trusted org/OU or unfamiliar, treat as active hijack. Identify what data stream (replication/log delivery/Storage) targeted that bucket name. 2) Contain: cut off the data stream at the source (pause replication / redirect log delivery), revoke the actor's credentials, and apply a data-perimeter SCP/VPC-endpoint policy denying writes to buckets in non-org accounts. Engage IR if the recreating account is external. 3) Hunt: enumerate all sinks/replication rules referencing the hijacked name, review recent GetBucketReplication/ListBuckets recon by the same principal, and audit which objects/logs were written after the recreate timestamp.
source:cloudtrail @eventSource:s3.amazonaws.com @evt.name:(DeleteBucket OR CreateBucket) @requestParameters.bucketName:*
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail  (organization trail spanning all accounts)
fields @timestamp, eventName, recipientAccountId, userIdentity.arn, requestParameters.bucketName
| filter eventSource = "s3.amazonaws.com" and eventName in ["DeleteBucket", "CreateBucket"] and not isPresent(errorCode)
| stats count_distinct(eventName) as distinctOps, count_distinct(recipientAccountId) as accounts, earliest(eventName) as firstOp, latest(eventName) as lastOp by requestParameters.bucketName
| filter distinctOps >= 2 and accounts >= 2
| sort accounts desc
CLOUD
sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource="s3.amazonaws.com" (eventName=DeleteBucket OR eventName=CreateBucket)
| search NOT errorCode=*
| stats earliest(_time) as firstTime latest(_time) as lastTime values(eventName) as ops dc(eventName) as opCount values(recipientAccountId) as accounts dc(recipientAccountId) as acctCount values(userIdentity.arn) as users values(sourceIPAddress) as src_ip by requestParameters.bucketName
| where opCount>=2 AND acctCount>=2
| eval windowSeconds=lastTime-firstTime
| sort - lastTime
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)

SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Command & Control. Storm-2603 SharePoint ToolShell exploitation: ToolPane.aspx/spinstall0.aspx + win.ini/web.config LFI probing AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound SharePoint requests matching the ToolShell chain used by Storm-2603 (CVE-2025-49704/49706/53770/53771) — the /_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx exploit endpoint and spinstall0.aspx web shell — alongside the win.ini/web.config local-file-inclusion probing the article calls out, and known attacker source IPs. Article-specific because it keys on the exact URIs and IPs tied to this intrusion, not generic web scanning. Rationale: Uses the exact ToolShell endpoint /_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx and spinstall0.aspx web shell plus the win.ini/web.config LFI strings named in the article, and attacker IPs 38.54.16.179 / 91.236.230.76 confirmed by Huntress as the ToolShell/web-shell source addresses. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/07/22/disrupting-active-exploitation-of-on-premises-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/microsoft-sharepoint-cve-2025-49704-cve-2025-49706-cve-2025-53770/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable/Rapid7) probing SharePoint for ToolShell
  • Internal red-team / pentest engagement replaying the ToolShell PoC
  • SharePoint health probes that legitimately request web.config paths
  • Security researchers fingerprinting the patch level from an allow-listed jump host
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.","192.168.") // scope to external; append your scanner IP allowlist e.g. and cIP !in ("<approved-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full W3CIISLog for the source IP — confirm a POST to ToolPane.aspx followed by a 200 on spinstall0.aspx or a machine-key theft attempt; check whether the SharePoint host is patched for CVE-2025-53770. 2) Contain: isolate the SharePoint server, rotate ASP.NET machine keys (mandatory post-ToolShell), and block the source IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search DeviceProcessEvents for w3wp.exe spawning cmd/powershell on that host and for msiexec pulls from *.workers.dev to catch the follow-on Velociraptor stage.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("38.54.16.179","91.236.230.76","65.38.121.226")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has "/_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx"
    or csUriStem has_any ("spinstall0.aspx","win.ini","web.config")
    or csUriQuery has_any ("win.ini","web.config")
    or cIP in ("38.54.16.179","91.236.230.76","65.38.121.226")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning command shell — ToolShell web-shell execution AIInstallation High
Detects the post-exploitation execution stage where the SharePoint IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawns cmd/powershell/msiexec/net after ToolShell web-shell drop. This is the pivot from web exploit to hands-on-keyboard for Storm-2603 and is distinct from generic Office-spawns-script logic. Rationale: w3wp.exe is the SharePoint IIS worker; it legitimately never spawns cmd/powershell/net, so a shell child is the highest-fidelity signal of ToolShell web-shell (spinstall0.aspx) execution described in the article. Distinct from the excluded Office-spawns-script rule. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/storm-2603-ransomware-campaign-targets-microsoft-sharepoint-in-2025-activity-and-ttp-analysis
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint timer/health jobs invoking stsadm or PowerShell during patching
  • Admin-driven SharePoint PSConfig upgrade that runs cmd/powershell under the app-pool identity
  • Monitoring agents that shell out under the IIS worker for inventory
  • Legitimate custom SharePoint solutions that call out to whoami/net for identity checks
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSConfig","stsadm","OWSTIMER") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — base64/encoded PowerShell, net user, or msiexec http pulls are hostile; benign PSConfig/stsadm activity is not. 2) Contain: isolate the SharePoint host and suspend the app-pool identity; preserve w3wp memory if IR needs it. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceName for adminbak account creation, msiexec from *.workers.dev, and cloudflared/code.exe tunnel to trace the full Storm-2603 chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","msiexec.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","msiexec.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Velociraptor deployed via msiexec from workers.dev (Storm-2603 SecurityCheck.msi / CVE-2025-6264) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Storm-2603 remote-access foothold: msiexec pulling v3.msi/ssh.msi/SecurityCheck.msi from *.workers.dev to install an outdated Velociraptor (0.73.4.0) abusing CVE-2025-6264, or execution of the confirmed SecurityCheck payload hashes. Article-specific to the tunnel infrastructure and MSI names. Rationale: Anchors on the exact msiexec install pattern (v3.msi/ssh.msi) from *.workers.dev documented by Huntress for this campaign and the two SecurityCheck.msi/.exe SHA256 hashes confirmed across two sources; silent MSI install from a Cloudflare Worker domain is not legitimate admin behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://docs.velociraptor.app/announcements/advisories/cve-2025-6264/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/pt-identifying-and-mitigating-potential-velociraptor-abuse/
ATT&CKT1219 T1105 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IR team deploying Velociraptor during an authorized engagement (verify it is not from workers.dev)
  • Developer testing an MSI hosted on a personal Cloudflare Worker
  • OpenSSH server install by IT from an internal repo (should not use workers.dev)
  • Software-deployment tooling that stages MSIs via a CDN URL
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("SCNotification.exe","CcmExec.exe") ) // exclude SCCM-driven MSI staging
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the download host is *.workers.dev and hash matches SecurityCheck.msi/.exe; check installed Velociraptor version (0.73.4.0 = CVE-2025-6264 abuse) and whether it runs as a SYSTEM service. 2) Contain: stop and remove the rogue Velociraptor service, isolate the host, and block the four workers.dev C2 domains at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: sweep the estate for the same MSI hashes and for velociraptor.exe services beaconing to update.githubtestbak.workers.dev / chat.hcqhajfv.workers.dev.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "msiexec.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("workers.dev","v3.msi","ssh.msi","SecurityCheck.msi"))
    or SHA256 in ("c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682","040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423")
    or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in ("c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682","040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("workers.dev","v3.msi","ssh.msi","SecurityCheck.msi")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Multiple parallel remote-access/tunnel tools on one host (Cloudflare tunnel + VS Code tunnel + TightVNC + Zoho + OpenSSH) AICommand & Control Medium
Correlates the co-occurrence of the several distinct remote-access channels Storm-2603 layered on a single host — cloudflared tunnels, VS Code 'code.exe tunnel', TightVNC, Zoho Assist, and OpenSSH — firing when two or more independent families appear on the same device. Targets the article's 'multiple remote access channels' and 'parallel activity' theme. Rationale: Keys on the exact remote-access stack the article and Huntress attribute to Storm-2603 (Cloudflare tunnels, code.exe tunnel --accept-server-license-terms, tvnserver.exe -service, Zoho Assist, OpenSSH via ssh.msi); requiring 2+ distinct families on one host suppresses single legit-tool noise and directly expresses the 'parallel/multiple channels' finding. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/
ATT&CKT1219 T1572 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using VS Code tunnels plus SSH on the same workstation
  • IT support running Zoho Assist while also having OpenSSH installed
  • Sanctioned use of cloudflared for an internal service on a server that also runs VNC
  • Sysadmin jump box that intentionally hosts several remote-access utilities
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("<approved-jumpbox-hostnames>") // exclude sanctioned admin jump hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the make_set of tools and their command lines — attacker use shows tunnels pointed at *.workers.dev, service-mode VNC, and MSI-installed OpenSSH within a tight window; developer use is interactive and internal. 2) Contain: kill the tunnel/agent processes, remove the services, and block the tunnel egress domains; disable any adminbak accounts on the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to Velociraptor install and Defender disablement on the same DeviceName to confirm Storm-2603 attribution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend Tool = case(
    FileName =~ "code.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel", "VSCodeTunnel",
    FileName =~ "cloudflared.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "cloudflared", "CloudflareTunnel",
    FileName =~ "tvnserver.exe", "TightVNC",
    ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ZohoAssist","ZA_Connect") or FileName startswith "ZA_", "ZohoAssist",
    FileName =~ "sshd.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "ssh.msi", "OpenSSH",
    "")
| where isnotempty(Tool)
| summarize Tools=make_set(Tool), ToolCount=dcount(Tool), Cmds=make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 8), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName
| where ToolCount >= 2   // 2+ distinct remote-access/tunnel families on one host = Storm-2603 multi-channel pattern
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend Tool = case(
    NewProcessName endswith "code.exe" and CommandLine has "tunnel", "VSCodeTunnel",
    NewProcessName endswith "cloudflared.exe", "CloudflareTunnel",
    NewProcessName endswith "tvnserver.exe", "TightVNC",
    CommandLine has_any ("ZohoAssist","ZA_Connect"), "ZohoAssist",
    NewProcessName endswith "sshd.exe" or CommandLine has "ssh.msi", "OpenSSH",
    "")
| where isnotempty(Tool)
| summarize Tools=make_set(Tool), ToolCount=dcount(Tool), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| where ToolCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@CommandLine:(*tunnel* OR *--accept-server-license-terms* OR *ssh.msi* OR *ZohoAssist* OR *ZA_Connect*) OR @Image:(*\cloudflared.exe OR *\Cloudflared.exe OR *\tvnserver.exe OR *\TVNServer.exe OR *\sshd.exe))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/(cloudflared|tvnserver|sshd)\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/(code\.exe.*tunnel|--accept-server-license-terms|ssh\.msi|ZohoAssist|ZA_Connect)/i)
| case { ImageFileName=/cloudflared/i | Tool:="CloudflareTunnel" ; ImageFileName=/tvnserver/i | Tool:="TightVNC" ; CommandLine=/code\.exe.*tunnel/i | Tool:="VSCodeTunnel" ; CommandLine=/ZohoAssist|ZA_Connect/i | Tool:="ZohoAssist" ; * | Tool:="OpenSSH" }
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=collect([Tool]))
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Storm-2603 rogue admin account creation (adminbak/adminbak2) and Domain Admins enumeration AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the Storm-2603 backdoor local admin accounts adminbak/adminbak2, additions to Administrators/Domain Admins, and the 'net1 group "domain admins" /do' reconnaissance the actor used. Ties privilege escalation and discovery to the exact account names from the campaign. Rationale: Uses the literal backdoor account name adminbak (and adminbak2) plus the exact 'net1 group "domain admins" /do' recon string documented by Huntress for this intrusion; a generic net user /add would be noisy, but the adminbak token makes this campaign-specific and high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/before-toolshell-exploring-storm-2603s-previous-ransomware-operations/
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1136.002 T1069.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk creating a genuinely named 'admin-backup' break-glass account (verify exact spelling adminbak)
  • Scheduled tooling that audits Domain Admins membership via 'net group'
  • Sysadmin adding a service account to local Administrators during a legit build
  • Identity governance scripts enumerating privileged groups
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine contains "domain admins" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BginfoScheduledTask.exe","audit.ps1")) // exclude sanctioned group-audit tooling
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the account is literally adminbak/adminbak2 and who the SubjectUserName (creator) is; correlate creation time with SharePoint exploit and Velociraptor install on the same host. 2) Contain: disable/delete the rogue accounts, force-reset any accounts added to Domain Admins, and revoke sessions/tickets for them. 3) Hunt: search DeviceLogonEvents and SigninLogs for interactive/remote logons by adminbak across the estate and for ADExplorer usage indicating broader domain recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("net.exe","net1.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "adminbak"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "domain admins"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "localgroup administrators"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (EventID == 4720 and TargetUserName has "adminbak")
    or (EventID in (4732, 4728, 4756) and (MemberName has "adminbak" or TargetUserName in~ ("Administrators","Domain Admins")))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, Activity, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, MemberName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windows Defender disablement prior to tunnel install (Storm-2603 defense evasion) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Storm-2603 defense-evasion step where Microsoft Defender real-time protection/services are disabled (Set-MpPreference, sc stop WinDefend, DisableAntiSpyware) immediately before Cloudflare/tunnel installation. Keys on the specific tamper commands rather than generic AV noise. Rationale: The article calls out defense-evasion via disabling protections, and Huntress documents Windows Defender disablement immediately before Cloudflare install; anchoring on the concrete tamper verbs (Set-MpPreference/stop WinDefend/DisableAntiSpyware) keeps this tighter than generic AV-off alerts. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/pt-identifying-and-mitigating-potential-velociraptor-abuse/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EDR migration where Defender is intentionally disabled before deploying a new agent
  • Sysadmin adding a legitimate Defender exclusion path during app troubleshooting
  • Imaging/build pipelines that toggle real-time monitoring temporarily
  • Third-party AV installer disabling Defender as part of setup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","AgentSetup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and user — Defender-off followed within minutes by cloudflared/msiexec-from-workers.dev is hostile; a sanctioned EDR migration ticket is not. 2) Contain: re-enable Defender/Sense, isolate the host, and snapshot for IR; block tunnel egress. 3) Hunt: check for a BYOVD driver load (unsigned/known-vulnerable driver) on the same host and for the Velociraptor service the actor installs after neutralising protections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Set-MpPreference","DisableRealtimeMonitoring","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableIOAVProtection"))
    or (FileName in~ ("sc.exe","net.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("stop WinDefend","stop Sense","config WinDefend"))
    or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "DisableAntiSpyware")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("Set-MpPreference","DisableRealtimeMonitoring","DisableBehaviorMonitoring"))
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("sc.exe","net.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("stop WinDefend","stop Sense"))
    or (NewProcessName endswith "reg.exe" and CommandLine has "DisableAntiSpyware")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Storm-2603 concurrent C2 egress to workers.dev tunnels and attacker IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Network/DNS pivot detecting beacons to the four Cloudflare Worker C2 domains (velo/update.githubtestbak/royal-boat-bf05/chat) and the attacker IPs used across this intrusion. Because the actors ran several tunnels in parallel, this surfaces the concurrent command channels distinct from the process-level detections. Rationale: All four workers.dev domains and IPs 38.54.16.179 / 91.236.230.76 are corroborated by Huntress as this campaign's Velociraptor/tunnel C2 and ToolShell source infrastructure; matching them exactly makes for near-zero-FP network IOCs and captures the parallel command channels. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/velociraptor-misuse-part-two-eye-of-the-storm • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/22/one-intrusion-two-cyberattackers-uncovering-parallel-threat-activity/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign internal service coincidentally hosted on a different *.workers.dev subdomain (these four are specific)
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance resolving the IOCs for lookup
  • Sandbox/detonation host replaying the C2 domains during analysis
  • Security researcher pivoting on the infrastructure from an allow-listed box
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection (velociraptor.exe/cloudflared.exe = confirmed hostile) and the internal host/source IP. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block all four domains and the three IPs at DNS and egress proxy, isolate resolving hosts. 3) Hunt: for each resolving host, pull the Velociraptor-install and Defender-disable detections and enumerate adminbak logons to scope the full Storm-2603 footprint.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("velo.qaubctgg.workers.dev","royal-boat-bf05.qgtxtebl.workers.dev","update.githubtestbak.workers.dev","chat.hcqhajfv.workers.dev")
    or RemoteIP in ("38.54.16.179","91.236.230.76","65.38.121.226")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("velo.qaubctgg.workers.dev","royal-boat-bf05.qgtxtebl.workers.dev","update.githubtestbak.workers.dev","chat.hcqhajfv.workers.dev")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423") or SHA1 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423") or MD5 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423") or SHA1 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423") or MD5 in~ ("649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["649bdaa38e60ede6d140bd54ca5412f1091186a803d3905465219053393f6421", "12f177290a299bae8a363f47775fb99f305bbdd56bbdfddb39595b43112f9fb7", "a29125333ad72138d299cc9ef09718ddb417c3485f6b8fe05ba88a08bb0e5023", "c74897b1e986e2876873abb3b5069bf1b103667f7f0e6b4581fbda3fd647a74a", "c70fafe5f9a3e5a9ee7de584dd024cb552443659f06348398d3873aa88fd6682", "040d7ee5b7bb0b978220be326804fa827f6284c8478a27af88c616fcacfeb423"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] VBScript creating hidden working directory and VBS payloads under C:\Users\Public\Documents · [LLM] Renamed curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe running from Public\Documents working directory · [LLM] ManageEngine Endpoint Central (UEMS) agent silently installed as final RMM payload · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Beacon/download to WhatsApp-VBS campaign C2 infrastructure (202.61.160.0/24 + 38.55.151.63) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
WhatsApp Desktop spawning WScript executing VBS from attachment Transfers dir AIDelivery High
Hunts the campaign's initial-access foothold: WScript.exe launched directly by WhatsApp Desktop (WhatsApp.Root.exe) or executing a .vbs/.vbe from the WhatsApp UWP package Transfers path. This is the exact process relationship Kaspersky documented confirming the financial-lure VBScript was run from the WhatsApp client. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim WhatsApp UWP package path (5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\...\Transfers) and parent WhatsApp.Root.exe from the article's process-tree analysis plus the .vbs/.vbe extension - a combination no benign workflow produces. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/ • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-uncovers-a-new-massive-campaign-spreading-malware-via-whatsapp
ATT&CKT1566 T1204.002 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate .vbs business automation a user genuinely received and ran via WhatsApp (rare in enterprise but possible in some SME workflows)
  • Security testing / red-team simulation of WhatsApp-delivered scripts
  • A user manually saving then double-clicking a benign VBS from chat (parent would be explorer.exe, not WhatsApp.Root.exe - reduces FP)
  • EDR/AV sandbox detonation of submitted samples on an analyst workstation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("devenv.exe","sense.exe") // exclude EDR sandbox/dev detonation hosts; tune to your analyst VLAN device group
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 of the VBS; check the file name against the campaign's financial-lure list (Financial Reports.vbs, Account Statement.vbs, Debt Statement.vbs, etc.) and look for the child wscript downloading to C:\Users\Public\Documents\. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the wscript.exe tree, and quarantine the VBS from the WhatsApp Transfers folder; reset the sending contact's WhatsApp session (account likely compromised). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same DeviceId for the working-dir creation under Public\Documents, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=0 registry write, and outbound connections to 202.61.160.0/24 / 38.55.151.63.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "WhatsApp.Root.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs", ".vbe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "cscript.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "WhatsApp.Root.exe"
    or CommandLine has @"\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\"
| where CommandLine has_any (".vbs", ".vbe")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WhatsApp Desktop Spawning WScript Executing VBS Attachment
id: 6f3c1a2e-9b54-4f7d-8c21-2a1d6e0b4f10
description: Detects WScript/CScript launched by WhatsApp Desktop or executing a VBS/VBE from the WhatsApp UWP package Transfers directory, matching the WhatsApp VBScript RMM campaign.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1566
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  selection_parent_or_path:
    - ParentImage|endswith: '\WhatsApp.Root.exe'
    - CommandLine|contains: '\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\'
  selection_ext:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.vbs'
      - '.vbe'
  condition: selection_img and selection_parent_or_path and selection_ext
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe) (@ParentImage:(*\\WhatsApp.Root.exe OR *\\whatsapp.root.exe) OR @CommandLine:*\\Packages\\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\*) @CommandLine:(*.vbs* OR *.vbe*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| (ParentBaseFileName=/whatsapp\.root\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/\\Packages\\5319275A\.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\/i)
| CommandLine=/\.(vbs|vbe)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=wscript.exe OR Processes.process_name=cscript.exe) AND (Processes.parent_process_name="WhatsApp.Root.exe" OR Processes.process="*\\Packages\\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\*") AND (Processes.process="*.vbs*" OR Processes.process="*.vbe*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=wscript.exe OR Processes.process_name=cscript.exe) AND (Processes.parent_process_name="WhatsApp.Root.exe" OR Processes.process="*\\Packages\\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\*") AND (Processes.process="*.vbs*" OR Processes.process="*.vbe*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
VBScript creating hidden working directory and VBS payloads under C:\Users\Public\Documents AIInstallation High
Hunts Stage 1 staging: WScript/CScript writing files into a randomized Temp_<random> or MSUpdate_<random> working directory under C:\Users\Public\Documents\, often flagged hidden+system. This is the campaign's payload-staging step prior to fetching the two secondary VBS scripts. Rationale: Uses the verbatim staging path C:\Users\Public\Documents\ plus the two documented randomized directory prefixes Temp_ and MSUpdate_, scoped to a wscript/cscript writer - benign software almost never drops VBS into Public\Documents under those name patterns. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1564.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that legitimately stage VBS helpers in Public\Documents (uncommon, but check vendor)
  • IT logon-script tooling writing temp VBS to a shared public path
  • Backup/imaging software that names temp folders Temp_<id> (would not be a wscript writer - excluded by process filter)
  • Software installers using Public\Documents as a shared scratch area
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Veeam\", @"\Backup\")) // drop known backup scratch paths if they surface
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Enumerate the contents of the flagged Public\Documents working directory; capture any .vbs/.vbe and check for renamed curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe (DLL-like names) inside it. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, delete/quarantine the working directory, and kill the parent wscript tree. 3) HUNT: Tie the same DeviceId back to a WhatsApp.Root.exe -> wscript launch (UC1) and forward to ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin registry change and 202.61.160.0/24 egress.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp_", @"\MSUpdate_") or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".vbe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Temp_", @"\MSUpdate_") or TargetFileExtension in~ ("vbs","vbe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WScript Staging Files in Hidden Public Documents Working Directory
id: c2b9d7a1-4e83-49f6-b0a2-7d5c1e9f3a44

Renamed curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe running from Public\Documents working directory AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's LOLBin masquerading: curl.exe or bitsadmin.exe copied into the working directory and renamed with DLL-like filenames, exposed via the OriginalFileName-vs-FileName mismatch while executing from C:\Users\Public\Documents\. Used to download the secondary VBS payloads and the RMM ZIP. Rationale: Pivots on the article's documented trick of copying curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe under DLL-like names in the working dir - the PE OriginalFileName stays curl/bitsadmin while the on-disk FileName differs, a near-zero-FP masquerade signal when scoped to Public\Documents. Sentinel falls back to path+download-flag heuristics since 4688 lacks OriginalFileName. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
ATT&CKT1036.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or admin manually copying curl.exe to a scratch dir and renaming it for testing
  • Portable-app launchers that bundle a renamed curl.exe
  • Software updaters shipping curl under a vendor-specific name (rarely in Public\Documents)
  • Sysmon OriginalFileName field unpopulated on very old binaries (causes misses, not FPs)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") // only keep LOLBins launched by the script host, dropping dev/admin manual copies
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the renamed binary's hash and full command line - extract the download URL it fetched (compare against 202.61.160.0/24, 38.55.151.63, baoxis.cc). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, quarantine the renamed LOLBin and any downloaded ZIP/VBS in the working dir. 3) HUNT: Look on the same host for the resulting UEMSAgent.msi/.mst install and the ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin registry write; sweep org for other hosts running curl/bitsadmin from Public\Documents.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName in~ ("curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where FileName !in~ ("curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Temp_", @"\MSUpdate_")
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://", "https://", "--url", "/transfer", "-o ", "--output")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Renamed curl/bitsadmin LOLBin Executing From Public Documents
id: a81e7c44-2f19-4c0b-9d6e-3b7a5e2c1f88
description: Detects curl.exe or bitsadmin.exe renamed (OriginalFileName/FileName mismatch) and executing from C:\Users\Public\Documents, the download mechanism in the WhatsApp VBScript RMM campaign.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1036.003
  - attack.t1105
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    OriginalFileName:
      - 'curl.exe'
      - 'bitsadmin.exe'
    Image|contains: '\Users\Public\Documents\'
  filter_realname:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_realname
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\* ) @OriginalFileName:(curl.exe OR bitsadmin.exe) -@Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\/i
| OriginalFilename=/^(curl|bitsadmin)\.exe$/i
| NOT (ImageFileName=/\\(curl|bitsadmin)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, OriginalFilename, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.original_file_name=curl.exe OR Processes.original_file_name=bitsadmin.exe) AND NOT (Processes.process_name=curl.exe OR Processes.process_name=bitsadmin.exe) AND Processes.process_path="*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.original_file_name Processes.process_path Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.original_file_name=curl.exe OR Processes.original_file_name=bitsadmin.exe) AND NOT (Processes.process_name=curl.exe OR Processes.process_name=bitsadmin.exe) AND Processes.process_path="*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.original_file_name Processes.process_path Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
UAC ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin disabled (set to 0) by Windows Script Host AIExploitation High
Detects the Stage 2 'VBS script 1' behaviour: a script-host process writing HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin (or EnableLUA) to 0 to suppress admin elevation prompts. Scoped to wscript/cscript or a Public\Documents writer so it isolates the campaign's UAC-weakening step. Rationale: Uses the exact registry path from the article's Table 2 (HKLM\...\Policies\System\ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin) corroborated by SOCRadar's note that the value is set to 0, scoped to a script-host writer so legitimate GPO/admin UAC changes are excluded. Falcon left blank: UAC policy value is not an ASEP and is not reliably carried in AsepValueUpdate FDR telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/
ATT&CKT1548.002 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GPO or Intune policy lowering UAC (initiating process would be svchost/gpsvc, not wscript - excluded)
  • Admin manually disabling UAC via a configuration script
  • Vendor installers that toggle UAC during setup (rare, and not script-host-driven)
  • Security baseline rollback tooling
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","svchost.exe","taskhostw.exe") // exclude policy-driven UAC changes
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the writer is wscript/cscript and correlate with a Public\Documents working dir on the same host; re-enable UAC immediately (set ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin back to 5, EnableLUA to 1). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, kill the script tree, and treat the host as elevated-compromise. 3) HUNT: Look for the follow-on UEMSAgent RMM install and any repeated ShellExecute runas elevation loops; sweep for the same registry write across the estate.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin","EnableLUA")
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Policies\System"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin","EnableLUA")
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: UAC ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin Disabled by Script Host
id: e4d2b6f0-7a31-4c98-bb15-9c0e2f7a83d2
description: Detects wscript/cscript setting ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin or EnableLUA to 0 under Policies\System, the UAC-weakening step in the WhatsApp VBScript RMM campaign.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

detection:

    TargetObject|endswith:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\\CurrentVersion\\Policies\\System\\ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin OR *\\CurrentVersion\\Policies\\System\\EnableLUA) @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe)

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Policies\\System*" AND (Registry.registry_value_name=ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin OR Registry.registry_value_name=EnableLUA) AND Registry.registry_value_data=0 by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beacon/download to WhatsApp-VBS campaign C2 infrastructure (202.61.160.0/24 + 38.55.151.63) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects host connections to the campaign's attacker-controlled UEMS/management-server IPs and download domains. Confirmed by SOCRadar; the 202.61.160.x range overlaps prior ValleyRAT/Gh0st RAT infrastructure. Fires on any endpoint reaching these IOCs, with the initiating process surfaced for triage. Rationale: All six IPs are second-source-confirmed (SOCRadar lists the same 202.61.160.x management-server set plus 38.55.151.63, with 202.61.160.201 tied to prior ValleyRAT/Gh0st RAT infra). Domains are kept as has_any enrichment from the article's IOC list. CIDR 202.61.160.0/24 covers all five .160 hosts in one clause. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/ • https://www.technadu.com/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-installs-manageengine-rmm-kaspersky-warns/629801/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher/analyst sandbox deliberately reaching the IOCs for study
  • Threat-intel scanning or proxy that proactively resolves IOC domains
  • Shared hosting reuse - 202.61.160.0/24 belongs to a provider that may also host benign sites (validate the exact host)
  • Legitimate use of oss-ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com (Alibaba OSS) by unrelated apps - validate the full sdcwww subdomain before alerting on the domain clause
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or RemoteIP in ("202.61.160.208","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.201","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63") // keep all IP hits; drop only browser hits to the shared-hosting Aliyun domain
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process - if it is wscript.exe, msiexec.exe, or a renamed curl/bitsadmin from Public\Documents, treat as confirmed; capture URL/port and bytes transferred. 2) CONTAIN: Block the IPs (and 202.61.160.0/24) and domains at the egress proxy/firewall, isolate the host. 3) HUNT: Pivot to the host's process tree for the WhatsApp->wscript chain, the UEMS RMM install, and the UAC registry change; sweep all hosts that resolved the IOC domains.
let c2ips = dynamic(["202.61.160.208","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.201","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63"]);
let c2domains = dynamic(["temu.baskwms.top","invoice.msopsa.top","baoxis.cc","sdcwww.oss-ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (c2domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2ips = dynamic(["202.61.160.208","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.201","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63"]);

ManageEngine Endpoint Central (UEMS) agent silently installed as final RMM payload AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's end goal: deployment of a preconfigured ManageEngine Endpoint Central agent (UEMSAgent.msi + attacker UEMSAgent.mst transform + DCAgentServerInfo.json) giving covert remote access. Scoped to script-host / Public\Documents-spawned installs so it isolates abuse from legitimate enterprise Endpoint Central rollouts. Rationale: Anchors on the exact RMM artifact names UEMSAgent.msi, the attacker UEMSAgent.mst transform, and DCAgentServerInfo.json (ManageEngine Endpoint Central) confirmed by SOCRadar, gated on a script-host/Public\Documents context so legitimate sanctioned Endpoint Central deployments (pushed by your own server via SYSTEM/services) don't fire. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-uses-fake.html
ATT&CKT1219 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned ManageEngine Endpoint Central agent rollout by your IT team (initiating process would be the EC server push / SYSTEM service, not wscript - the context gate excludes it)
  • Endpoint Central self-update writing agent files under Program Files (not Public\Documents)
  • An admin manually staging UEMSAgent.msi in a downloads/temp folder for testing
  • MSP-managed devices where Endpoint Central is the legitimate RMM (validate the management server in DCAgentServerInfo.json against your known UEMS server)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dcagentregister.exe","dcagenttrayicon.exe","services.exe") // exclude legitimate Endpoint Central self-managed agent file writes
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open DCAgentServerInfo.json and the .mst transform - compare the configured management server against your sanctioned Endpoint Central server; if it points to 202.61.160.0/24 / 38.55.151.63 it is malicious. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, stop/uninstall the rogue UEMS agent and its service, kill active remote sessions, and block the management-server IPs. 3) HUNT: Trace back to the WhatsApp->wscript chain and UAC change on the host, and sweep the org for any UEMSAgent install whose server config is not your own.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("UEMSAgent.msi","UEMSAgent.mst","DCAgentServerInfo.json")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","msiexec.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
    or FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "UEMSAgent" or CommandLine has "DCAgentServerInfo"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "cscript.exe" or CommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects creation of UEMSAgent.msi/UEMSAgent.mst/DCAgentServerInfo.json by a script host or from Public\Documents, the final RMM payload of the WhatsApp VBScript campaign.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
