PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or SHA1 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or MD5 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or SHA1 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or MD5 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

// Article-specific bespoke detection — A VBScript campaign distributed through WhatsApp deploying RMM software
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("reports.vbs", "confirmation.vbs", "list.vbs", "statement.vbs", "aus.vbs", "bank.vbs", "anda.vbs", "whatsapp.root.exe", "curl.exe", "setup1.vbs", "setup.bat", "uemsagent.msi", "form.vbs", "applicationform1.vbs", "sheet.vbs") or FolderPath has_any ("C:\Windows\System32\WScript.exe", "\AppData\Local\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\", "C:\Users\Public\Documents\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

OpenRemote cross-realm alarm DELETE: single client deleting alarms in >1 realm (IDOR) AIExploitation High
Hunts the core removeAlarms IDOR (GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf): a single authenticated client issuing DELETE requests to /api/{realm}/alarm for more than one distinct realm. In OpenRemote a normal tenant user operates within exactly one realm, so any source touching alarm deletions across multiple realm paths is the defining cross-tenant exploitation signal. Rationale: Pivots on the exact vulnerable shape — DELETE to /api/{realm}/alarm (PoC: DELETE /api/smartcity/alarm) — and on the realm path segment that OpenRemote routing confirms is the first /api/ token. dcount(realm)>1 per client is the cleanest expression of cross-tenant IDOR with no need for an external realm-to-user ACL mapping. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf • https://docs.openremote.io/docs/architecture/manager-endpoints-and-file-paths/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/io.openremote/openremote-manager/CVE-2026-41166/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Master-realm superadmin legitimately managing alarms across all tenants (OpenRemote's superuser operates cross-realm by design)
  • MSP / managed-service operator account provisioned with multi-realm scope
  • Automated alarm-retention/housekeeping service account with cross-realm permissions
  • Multiple tenants' admins egressing through a shared corporate NAT IP so distinct legit users collapse to one SourceIP when SourceUserName is not forwarded by the proxy
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the client (SourceUserName if forwarded, else SourceIP) and list the realms hit and how many DELETEs returned 2xx. Pull the caller's actual home realm/role from OpenRemote Keycloak; a tenant user with WRITE_ALARMS_ROLE hitting other realms is exploitation, not admin work. 2) Contain: revoke/disable the offending Keycloak account and its sessions, block the SourceIP at the proxy/WAF, and confirm OpenRemote Manager is upgraded to >= 1.24.2. 3) Hunt: enumerate which victim realms lost alarms, restore from DB backup, and review the same client for prior 404-probing (enumeration) and 401/403 boundary-testing in the preceding hour.

OpenRemote high-volume alarm DELETE to /api/*/alarm (mass destruction / scripted abuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single client issuing a high volume of successful DELETE requests to the OpenRemote alarm endpoint in a short window — the impact phase of the removeAlarms IDOR where an attacker scripts repeated bulk deletes to permanently destroy safety-critical and security alarms. Note a single request can carry many IDs in its body, so request-rate is a conservative lower bound on damage. Rationale: Targets the article's bulk-delete impact using the concrete endpoint (/api/{realm}/alarm) and successful (2xx) responses. Threshold of 20 successful DELETEs per 10 min flags scripted/automated destruction; because the IDs live in the request body (not logged), request count is a deliberate proxy and pairs with the cross-realm UC for confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf • https://docs.openremote.io/docs/architecture/manager-endpoints-and-file-paths/

OpenRemote alarm-endpoint authorization-failure cascade then success (IDOR boundary probing) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects the probe-and-exploit pattern characteristic of IDOR discovery: a single client receiving multiple 401/403 responses on DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm and then succeeding (2xx) within the same short window. This surfaces an attacker systematically testing which realms/IDs they can reach before landing a working cross-tenant delete. Rationale: Uses the article's stated probe semantics (authorization errors on restricted realms followed by successes on exploitable ones) against the specific DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm endpoint. Same-bucket failure+success per client is a high-signal boundary-testing shape that generic alarm activity does not produce. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A partially-privileged user who legitimately hits some forbidden alarms (403) then deletes ones they own (2xx)
  • A buggy/retrying API client that re-sends after token refresh produces 401 then 200
  • A Keycloak role/permission change mid-session flipping 403 to 200
  • Pen-test / authorized vulnerability scan against the OpenRemote instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: order the client's requests by time and confirm the 401/403 -> 2xx transition is against different realm IDs (probing) rather than one resource retried after auth refresh. 2) Contain: disable the account/sessions and block the SourceIP if probing across realms is confirmed; verify the instance is patched to >= 1.24.2. 3) Hunt: pull the full request sequence for this client to map which realms were probed vs. successfully deleted, then check for 404-based ID enumeration and high-volume deletes from the same source.

| sort by AuthFailures desc
source:nginx @http.method:DELETE @http.url_details.path:/api/*/alarm @http.status_code:(401 OR 403)

OpenRemote alarm-ID enumeration via 404-response probing across realms AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects cross-tenant alarm enumeration: a single client generating many 404 responses on DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm, optionally while rotating realm paths. The advisory states presence of sequential auto-increment alarm IDs is confirmed by 404-vs-200 responses, so a burst of 404s on this endpoint is the discovery footprint that precedes targeted destruction. Rationale: Built directly on the advisory's enumeration mechanism (sequential @GeneratedValue IDs confirmed by 404 vs 200). A high 404 count on DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm from one client (amplified when realm_count>1) is a distinct discovery pivot separate from the impact/volume detections. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf • https://docs.openremote.io/docs/architecture/manager-endpoints-and-file-paths/

  • Synthetic monitoring / health-check probes repeatedly calling the alarm endpoint
  • Load/performance testing against a staging realm
  • A broken integration referencing stale alarm IDs after a data purge
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the 404 burst is DELETE (not benign GET) on /api/{realm}/alarm and whether realm_count>1; sequential 404s from one client against IDs they never created indicates enumeration. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP and disable the account if it is a tenant user probing foreign realms; ensure the instance is upgraded to >= 1.24.2. 3) Hunt: correlate this client forward in time for the first 2xx deletes (successful exploitation) and the authorization-failure cascade, and review whether any victim realm alarms were ultimately destroyed.

Archive (TAR/ZIP) upload to Langflow BaseFileComponent file API (CVE-2026-55447 delivery) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts POST uploads of tar/zip archives to Langflow's file-ingestion endpoints (/api/v1/files/upload, /api/v2/files) that feed BaseFileComponent-derived nodes (Read File, Docling, Unstructured). This is the delivery vector for the symlink-TAR arbitrary-file-read in CVE-2026-55447, where a crafted archive is uploaded to a RAG ingestion flow. Rationale: Uses the article's named ingestion path (BaseFileComponent file upload) plus archive extensions; the endpoint strings /api/v1/files/upload and /api/v2/files are Langflow-specific upload routes that feed the vulnerable nodes. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/security-bulletin-path-traversal-vulnerability-file-processing-components-allows-unauthorized-file-system-access-and-potential-remote-code-execution
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users uploading zipped document bundles into a RAG ingestion flow
  • Backup/export archives POSTed to the files API by an integration
  • Automated data-loader jobs bulk-uploading tar-packaged corpora
  • Security scanners / DAST tools probing the upload endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the uploaded archive from Langflow storage and inspect TAR members with `tar -tvf` — flag any entry whose type is symlink/hardlink or whose linkname is an absolute path (/etc, /root, /.ssh, secret_key). 2) Contain: if malicious members present, quarantine the archive, revoke the uploader's session/API token, and confirm Langflow is patched to >=1.9.2. 3) Hunt: pivot to the Langflow host and check whether the worker process subsequently read credential files (UC 'credential access') or made outbound connections (UC 'exfiltration').
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has_any ("/api/v1/files/upload", "/api/v2/files", "/api/v1/files/")
| where FileName has_any (".tar", ".tgz", ".tar.gz", ".zip") or HttpResponseHeaderContentType has_any ("tar", "zip", "octet-stream")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, Url, HttpMethod, FileName, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow worker reads JWT secret_key / OS credential files via symlink-TAR (CVE-2026-55447) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the Langflow Python worker (python/uvicorn/gunicorn/langflow) opening sensitive files outside its working tree — the JWT secret_key file, /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, ~/.ssh, ~/.aws/credentials — which is the core arbitrary-file-read primitive of CVE-2026-55447 that leads to JWT forgery and RCE. Rationale: Directly targets the article's exploit: the worker reading Langflow's secret_key (JWT signing secret) plus the reviewer-supplied credential paths (/etc/shadow, ~/.ssh, ~/.aws/credentials). A RAG worker opening /etc/shadow or a secret_key outside its config context is near-zero in normal operation. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/security-bulletin-path-traversal-vulnerability-file-processing-components-allows-unauthorized-file-system-access-and-potential-remote-code-execution
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow legitimately reading its OWN secret_key from LANGFLOW_CONFIG_DIR at startup (scope to reads of paths outside the config dir)
  • An operator's interactive python shell on the same host reading ~/.ssh for git/ssh ops
  • Backup agent running under the same service account touching /etc or /root
  • Config-management (Ansible/Salt) python modules reading /etc/passwd
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "secret_key" and FolderPath has_any ("/.cache/langflow/", "/app/langflow/", "/root/.cache/langflow/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the accessing PID is the Langflow web/worker process (not an admin shell) and that the accessed path is OUTSIDE Langflow's configured secret dir; check the ingested vector store for the leaked file contents. 2) Contain: rotate the Langflow secret_key (invalidates forged JWTs), force logout of all sessions, rotate any credentials the file exposed (SSH keys, AWS keys), and patch to >=1.9.2. 3) Hunt: search for anomalous JWT-authenticated flow creations (esp. Python Interpreter nodes) and for the RCE/exfil UCs on this host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|langflow)$"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/shadow", "/etc/passwd", "/.ssh/", "/.aws/credentials", "secret_key", "/root/")
     or FileName in~ ("shadow", "passwd", "id_rsa", "credentials", "secret_key")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc

Langflow Python worker spawns shell / network LOLBin (CVE-2026-55447 Python Interpreter node RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the Langflow worker process (python/uvicorn/gunicorn/langflow) spawning an interactive shell or network tool (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, socat). After JWT forgery, the CVE-2026-55447 chain achieves RCE via a Python Interpreter node whose payload shells out — a web/RAG worker parenting /bin/sh is highly anomalous. Rationale: Grounded in the article's stated RCE step — a Python Interpreter node running attacker code. A Langflow web/worker process (python/uvicorn/gunicorn) is not expected to fork shells or curl/nc; parent+child pairing turns generic execution into intent. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://gbhackers.com/langflow-rce-flaw/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow components that legitimately shell out (e.g. a shell-command tool node an operator deliberately configured)
  • Container entrypoint/health-check scripts where uvicorn is PID1 and runs `sh -c`
  • python-based subprocess calls in custom components (e.g. calling `curl` for a webhook)
  • CI/agent tasks running under the same service account
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/healthcheck", "docker-entrypoint", "livenessProbe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child process command line and the parent Langflow PID; determine if a Python Interpreter / shell-command node was recently added to a flow. 2) Contain: kill the child process tree, isolate the host, rotate the Langflow secret_key and any exposed credentials, and block outbound to any C2 the child contacted. 3) Hunt: enumerate all flows for Python Interpreter nodes with suspicious code, review who created/edited flows via the API (forged-JWT accounts), and check for persistence (cron, systemd, SSH authorized_keys) dropped by the child.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|langflow)$"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","perl","ruby")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|langflow)$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|curl|wget|nc|ncat|socat|perl|ruby)$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow credential read followed by outbound egress within 5 min (CVE-2026-55447 exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a Langflow worker reading a sensitive credential/secret file with an outbound public network connection from the same worker within 5 minutes. Catches post-exploitation exfiltration of the stolen JWT secret_key or OS credentials in the CVE-2026-55447 chain. Rationale: Chains the article's two decisive artifacts — the worker reading secret_key/OS credentials and then egressing — inside a tight 5-minute window, which the reviewer flagged as the missing post-exploitation context. The temporal + same-host + same-process-family join keeps FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://cyberpress.org/langflow-ai-pipeline-rce-exploited/
ATT&CKT1041 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow legitimately reading its own secret_key at startup then making outbound LLM/API calls (OpenAI, vector DB) within 5 min
  • Backup agent reading /etc or ~/.ssh then uploading to cloud storage
  • Telemetry/update agent under same account phoning home post config-read
  • A RAG flow that reads an allow-listed local doc and calls an external embedding API
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has_any ("openai.com", "anthropic.com", "cohere.ai", "pinecone.io", "huggingface.co")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the read path is genuinely out-of-scope (not Langflow's own config secret_key) and that the outbound IP is not a known LLM/vector-DB provider; capture bytes-out. 2) Contain: block the destination IP/domain, isolate the host, rotate secret_key and all exposed credentials, and revoke active JWT sessions. 3) Hunt: review the vector store for leaked file content, enumerate other hosts running <1.9.2 Langflow, and check for inbound flow-creation from forged-JWT sessions.

Langflow worker creates symlink in temp dir during TAR extraction (CVE-2026-55447 traversal setup) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the Langflow worker creating symbolic links / files in /tmp or /var/tmp during BaseFileComponent TAR extraction — the actual _unpack_bundle attack step where a malicious tar's symlink member is written to disk pointing at an out-of-tree credential path before process_files() reads the target. Rationale: Implements the reviewer's traversal-setup hypothesis using the article's _unpack_bundle mechanism: the worker writes tar members into a temp extraction dir; auditd symlink syscalls are the accurate telemetry, with DeviceFileEvents/FileWritten as best-effort where symlink syscall logging is absent. Names/'..' filter narrows to credential-targeting members. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ccv6-r384-xp75
ATT&CKT1083 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate document bundles that happen to contain files named 'credentials.docx' or similar
  • python-based build/test tooling writing scratch files to /tmp
  • Antivirus or backup software staging files in /var/tmp
  • Application caches or session temp files created by the same worker
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/pip-", "/tmp/tmp", "/var/tmp/systemd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: locate the created temp file and check whether it is a symlink (`ls -l`) and where its target points; correlate with a preceding archive upload (UC 'archive upload'). 2) Contain: if it symlinks to a credential path, quarantine the source archive, kill the worker if mid-exploit, and patch to >=1.9.2 (which rejects symlink/hardlink tar members). 3) Hunt: check whether the symlink target was subsequently read (UC 'credential access') and whether egress followed (UC 'exfiltration'); audit all recent uploads to BaseFileComponent flows.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|langflow)$"
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/", "/var/tmp/")
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)(passwd|shadow|id_rsa|credentials|secret_key)" or FolderPath has ".."
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "type=SYSCALL"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("syscall=symlink", "syscall=symlinkat")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/tmp/", "/var/tmp/")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("python", "uvicorn", "gunicorn", "langflow")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow IDOR endpoint access — POST to /api/v1/responses (CVE-2026-55255) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces POST traffic to the Langflow OpenAI-compatible endpoints affected by CVE-2026-55255 (/api/v1/responses, /api/v2/workflow, /api/v1/run*). An authenticated attacker abuses the IDOR by passing a victim's flow UUID in the request body; web access logs reveal which authenticated principals and source IPs are reaching these endpoints and whether the server returned 200 (flow executed). Rationale: Uses the exact affected routes named in the advisory (/api/v1/responses, plus /api/v2/workflow and /api/v1/run* that the fix also hardened) and the POST method from the PoC curl. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty because EDR/FDR telemetry cannot see the HTTP request path/body of a self-hosted Langflow app — this detection lives in web access logs. Cross-checked against GitLab Advisory DB and OpenCVE which confirm CWE-639 and the affected route. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55255/ • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?vendor=langflow
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow users invoking their own flows via the OpenAI-compatible /api/v1/responses endpoint
  • Application SDKs / agent frameworks calling the endpoint at high volume as designed
  • CI/CD pipelines or synthetic monitors exercising the Langflow API
  • Kubernetes/ELB health-check probes hitting the endpoint
  • Internal integration services that legitimately run shared flows
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "kube-probe" and csUserAgent !has "ELB-HealthChecker" and csUserAgent !has "Datadog"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the distinct (csUsername, cIP, csUriStem, scStatus) tuples; flag principals running flows they don't normally run and any source IP outside the known app/integration ranges. 200 responses mean the flow actually executed. 2) Contain: if a non-owner principal received 200s, rotate that user's API key, and upgrade the Langflow instance to >=1.9.1 (CVE-2026-55255 fixed in 1.9.1 / PR #12832) which forces cross-user lookups to 404. 3) Hunt: pivot the same source IP/user across /api/v2/workflow and /api/v1/run*, and review whether sensitive flows (those handling secrets/PII) were among the executed flow IDs.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/api/v1/responses", "/api/v2/workflow") or csUriStem startswith "/api/v1/run"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SourceIP = cIP, User = csUsername, csMethod, csUriStem, Status = scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow IDOR enumeration — single source fan-out to /api/v1/responses (CVE-2026-55255) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single authenticated user or source IP issuing more than 20 POSTs to /api/v1/responses within a 5-minute window — the signature of automated enumeration of victim flow UUIDs to find and execute flows owned by other users, as enabled by CVE-2026-55255. Rationale: Implements the reviewer's >20-requests-in-5m aggregation against the exact IDOR endpoint. Rapid sequential POSTs to /api/v1/responses with varying flow IDs in the body is the only way to brute-force/enumerate other users' flow UUIDs, since the helper leaks no 403-vs-404 oracle before the 1.9.1 fix. Threshold tier because it carries a concrete temporal/volume condition. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55255/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Batch agent applications legitimately running many flow executions per minute
  • Load/performance testing against the Langflow API
  • A shared service account fronting many end users so all volume attributes to one principal/IP
  • Reverse proxy collapsing many clients behind one egress IP (NAT)
  • Scheduled bulk-inference jobs that fire dozens of flow runs together
Suppression filter
| where User !in~ ("svc-langflow-batch") and csUserAgent !has "k6" and csUserAgent !has "Locust"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the bursting principal/IP is a known batch/service identity; inspect the spread of scStatus — a mix of 404s turning into 200s strongly indicates UUID enumeration finding valid flows. 2) Contain: throttle/block the offending source at the proxy/WAF, disable or rotate the abused API key, and upgrade Langflow to >=1.9.1. 3) Hunt: enumerate which flow IDs returned 200 for this principal and cross-reference flow ownership; check the same source against /api/v2/workflow and /api/v1/run* for parallel enumeration.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem == "/api/v1/responses"
| summarize RequestCount = count(), DistinctStatuses = make_set(scStatus), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP = cIP, User = csUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where RequestCount > 20   // empirical: legit clients rarely exceed ~20 flow executions / 5m; enumeration spikes well above
| order by RequestCount desc

| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST AND Web.url="*/api/v1/responses*" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| where count > 20
| sort - count
Asset exposure — Langflow instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-55255 (<1.9.1) AIReconnaissance High
Deterministic exposure hunt: enumerates managed hosts whose installed Langflow version is flagged vulnerable to CVE-2026-55255 by the threat-and-vulnerability inventory. Prioritises internet-facing/authenticated instances for upgrade to 1.9.1 before the IDOR can be exploited. Rationale: Pure IOC-driven exposure match on the article's CVE id (CVE-2026-55255) against the real DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities / CIM Vulnerabilities CveId column — zero ambiguity, no behavioural guesswork. Defender query enriches with IsInternetFacing to prioritise the highest-risk Langflow hosts. Confirmed affected range (<1.9.1) and fix (1.9.1) via GitLab Advisory DB. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55255/ • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/releases
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to >=1.9.1 but scanner inventory not yet refreshed (stale snapshot)
  • Langflow Desktop builds vs server builds reported under the same software name
  • Air-gapped/internal-only instances flagged as if internet-facing
  • Decommissioned VMs still present in the inventory
  • Version string parsed from a side-by-side/secondary install rather than the running service
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely <1.9.1 and that the Langflow service is actually running and reachable (prioritise IsInternetFacing == true). 2) Contain: schedule/expedite upgrade to Langflow 1.9.1 (CVE-2026-55255 fix, PR #12832); for instances that cannot be patched immediately, restrict the /api/v1/responses, /api/v2/workflow and /api/v1/run* routes at the proxy to trusted principals. 3) Hunt: for each exposed host, run the UC_1/UC_2 web-log hunts over the exposure window to determine whether the IDOR was already exercised before patching.

| where CveId == "CVE-2026-55255"

| order by IsInternetFacing desc

Craft CMS resource-js Host/X-Forwarded-Host poisoning (CVE-2026-55791) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts unauthenticated requests to Craft's /actions/app/resource-js endpoint where a single client cycles multiple distinct Host header values, the fingerprint of trustedHosts:['any'] abuse poisoning $baseUrl. Article-specific: only this endpoint reflects attacker-controlled content as application/javascript. Rationale: Anchored on the exact vulnerable URI 'app/resource-js' and the article's stated mechanism of poisoning the Host header to manipulate $baseUrl; dcount(Host) per client avoids needing the victim's domain (no placeholder) while flagging the header-rewriting pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh/
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate multi-domain Craft install serving several front-end hostnames from one CDN/proxy egress IP
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors probing the site with varied Host headers
  • Security scanners (Burp, Nuclei) run by the org's own pentest team
  • Shared NAT egress where many real users appear as one SrcIpAddr
  • CDN revalidation requests carrying origin-shield Host values
Suppression filter
| where DstHostname !in ("monitoring.internal")  // append known synthetic-monitor egress hosts after baselining
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull HostSamples for the flagged SrcIpAddr — confirm values are IP literals, internal names, or attacker domains rather than the site's real hostnames; check response status/size on those requests. 2) Contain: in config/general.php set trustedHosts to the explicit allowed host(s) and upgrade craftcms/cms to >=4.17.9 / >=5.9.15; block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC for outbound fetches from the web-server process and to admin plugin-install POSTs from the same window.
let lookback = 24h;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url has "resource-js"
| extend HostHeader = tostring(HttpHostName)
| where isnotempty(HostHeader)
| summarize DistinctHosts = dcount(HostHeader), HostSamples = make_set(HostHeader, 10), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where DistinctHosts > 3   // one client cycling >3 distinct Host values at resource-js = header fuzzing / baseUrl poisoning
| order by DistinctHosts desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Web.http_host) as distinct_hosts, values(Web.http_host) as host_values, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*app/resource-js*" OR Web.url="*action=app/resource-js*") by Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where distinct_hosts > 3 | sort - distinct_hosts
Craft CMS trustedHosts bypass via localhost/127.0.0.1 Host header from external IP AIDelivery Medium
Detects requests to Craft's resource-js endpoint where the Host or X-Forwarded-Host header claims to be localhost/127.0.0.1/::1 but the source IP is public — a direct attempt to defeat front-end Host validation against the trustedHosts:['any'] default. Single occurrence is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable endpoint plus the concrete loopback literals attackers supply to spoof a trusted origin; pairing a loopback Host with a public source IP is behaviour no legitimate client produces, making it a low-FP alerting candidate. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh/
ATT&CKT1190 T1199
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal health-check that wrongly egresses through a public IP while sending Host: localhost
  • Misconfigured reverse proxy forwarding a literal localhost Host upstream
  • Container-to-container probe traversing a public NAT
  • Pentest/scanner deliberately fuzzing Host headers
  • Load balancer health probe rewritten to 127.0.0.1
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SrcIpAddr is genuinely external and not an internal monitor NAT'd to a public address; review HTTP status/size of the response. 2) Contain: set explicit trustedHosts in config/general.php, upgrade craftcms/cms to >=4.17.9 / >=5.9.15, and block the source IP. 3) Hunt: check for outbound fetches from php-fpm/nginx to internal or metadata IPs and for any /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin POSTs in the following minutes.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "resource-js"
| extend HostHeader = tolower(tostring(HttpHostName))
| where HostHeader has_any ("localhost","127.0.0.1","[::1]","::1","0.0.0.0")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)) and SrcIpAddr !in ("::1","127.0.0.1")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Blind SSRF: Craft web-server process fetching internal/cloud-metadata hosts AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the SSRF half of CVE-2026-55791 — Craft's Guzzle client (running under php-fpm/nginx/httpd) making outbound connections to RFC1918, link-local, or the 169.254.169.254 cloud-metadata endpoint after $baseUrl poisoning. Article-specific: the vuln forces this Guzzle fetch with ALLOW_REDIRECTS=true. Rationale: Targets the article's stated server-side fetch (Craft::createGuzzleClient()->get($url)) by pivoting on the web-server process making unexpected internal/metadata connections; the 169.254.169.254 focus is corroborated by Craft's related metadata-SSRF CVE-2026-27129, and DB ports are excluded to suppress routine backend traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-27129/
ATT&CKT1090 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • php-fpm calling an internal microservice/API on an allowed private host (8080/9200)
  • nginx reverse-proxying to an internal app server
  • Legitimate use of an internal package mirror or Composer proxy
  • App-level health checks hitting internal services
  • Sidecar/service-mesh proxies on private IPs
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "10." and RemotePort == 9200)  // example: drop known internal Elasticsearch; extend with allowed internal services after baselining
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and the InitiatingProcessId — was 169.254.169.254 or an internal admin port hit, and is there a matching resource-js request in web logs? 2) Contain: rotate any cloud IAM credentials reachable via metadata if 169.254.169.254 was contacted, set explicit trustedHosts, and patch craftcms/cms. 3) Hunt: review web logs for resource-js Host poisoning from the originating window and for outbound connections to attacker-owned public IPs reflecting fetched JS.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254"   // cloud metadata — classic blind-SSRF target (cf. CVE-2026-27129)
     or (RemoteIPType in ("Private","LinkLocal") and RemotePort in (80,443,8080,8000,8443,9200,2375,6379))
| where RemotePort !in (3306,5432,1433,11211)   // strip routine DB / memcache backend traffic
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

Craft CMS 1-click RCE: plugin-install POST riding a poisoned resource-js JS load AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the cache-poisoning payoff of CVE-2026-55791 — an admin browser that loaded the resource-js response as application/javascript then, within minutes from the same client, POSTs to /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin (session riding using window.Craft.csrfTokenValue). This is the RCE step, not a generic CSRF check. Rationale: Uses the two concrete article URIs ('resource-js' returning application/javascript, and 'actions/plugins/install-plugin' POST) plus the same-client temporal link the cache-poisoning-to-session-riding chain requires; plugin install is a rare CP action so the correlation is high-fidelity and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh/

Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Automated CI/deploy tooling that installs plugins via the CP from a fixed IP
  • Penetration test reproducing the chain
  • Admin behind same NAT as the resource-js request during routine work
  • Plugin Store updates triggering install-plugin during a CP session
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "CraftDeployBot"  // exclude known CI deploy automation user-agent after confirming it
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the resource-js response served to that client was attacker-controlled (external Host header, unexpected size/hash) versus the legitimate cached asset; identify the admin account tied to the session. 2) Contain: disable/inspect the installed plugin, force-logout and rotate the admin session + CSRF, set explicit trustedHosts, and patch to >=4.17.9 / >=5.9.15. 3) Hunt: review the file system for newly written plugin/PHP files and the web-server process for child processes or outbound C2 following the install.

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

Crossplane package installed by mutable tag instead of immutable digest AIInstallation High
Hunts Kubernetes API audit logs for pkg.crossplane.io Provider/Configuration/Function installs whose spec.package references a version tag rather than an @sha256 digest. This is the exact precondition GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r requires: when a package is pulled by tag, a malicious/compromised OCI registry can serve a correctly-signed image for cosign verification and then swap in unsigned content for the actual pull. Rationale: Built directly on the advisory's stated exploit precondition #2 ('Install packages using tag references rather than digests'). The detection keys on the real Crossplane API (pkg.crossplane.io Provider/Configuration/Function, spec.package) and the digest sentinel '@sha256:' that the fix mandates; absence of the digest is exactly what makes an install TOCTOU-exposed. Corroborated against the GHSA, the GitLab advisory mirror, and Crossplane's ImageConfig/package docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/crossplane/crossplane/v2/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r/ • https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/packages/image-configs/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GitOps/Argo/Flux pipelines that pin Crossplane packages to a semantic-version tag (e.g. provider-aws:v1.20.0) rather than a digest — common and benign in many shops
  • Platform-team installs from the org's own trusted internal registry where tag mutability is acceptable
  • Dev/sandbox clusters where engineers iterate on packages by floating tag
  • Initial cluster bootstrap installing first-party Upbound/Crossplane marketplace packages by tag
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style bots bumping a package tag during routine upgrades
Suppression filter
| where not (PackageRef startswith "xpkg.upbound.io/upbound/" or PackageRef startswith "xpkg.crossplane.io/")   // keep third-party / org-uncontrolled registries (advisory precondition #3), drop trusted first-party marketplace
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending Provider/Configuration object and its spec.package. Confirm whether the registry host is one the org controls (advisory precondition #3) and whether an ImageConfig with cosign verification matches that image. A tag-pinned package from a third-party registry under cosign verification is the high-risk case. 2) Contain: re-pin the package to the resolved immutable digest (spec.package: repo@sha256:...) and ensure Crossplane is on a fixed build (v2.3.3 / v2.2.3 or later); for vulnerable builds, prefer digest references org-wide until upgraded. 3) Hunt: inventory all pkg.crossplane.io resources still on tags, review the installed package revisions' Verified condition for skipped/incomplete status, and check whether the registry served differing digests for verify vs pull around the install time.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create", "update", "patch")
| extend ObjRef = todynamic(ObjectRef)
| where tostring(ObjRef.apiGroup) == "pkg.crossplane.io"
| where tostring(ObjRef.resource) in ("providers", "configurations", "functions")
| extend ReqObj = todynamic(RequestObject)
| extend PackageRef = tostring(ReqObj.spec.package)
| where isnotempty(PackageRef) and PackageRef !contains "@sha256:"   // not digest-pinned => mutable tag => TOCTOU-exposed
| extend Actor = tostring(todynamic(User).username)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, Verb, Kind = tostring(ObjRef.resource), ObjectName = tostring(ObjRef.name), PackageRef, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Crossplane Package Installed By Mutable Tag Without Digest Pin
id: 7a3c1e8b-2f4d-4c9a-b6e1-9d2f5a1c3e47
description: Detects creation/update of a Crossplane Provider, Configuration or Function whose spec.package uses a mutable tag rather than an immutable @sha256 digest, the precondition for the GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r signature-verification TOCTOU.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r
  - https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/packages/image-configs/

logsource:
  product: kubernetes
  service: audit
detection:
  selection:
    verb:
      - create
      - update
      - patch
    objectRef.apiGroup: 'pkg.crossplane.io'
    objectRef.resource:
      - 'providers'
      - 'configurations'
      - 'functions'
  filter_digest:
    requestObject.spec.package|contains: '@sha256:'
  condition: selection and not filter_digest
level: low
source:kubernetes.audit @objectRef.apiGroup:pkg.crossplane.io @objectRef.resource:(providers OR configurations OR functions) @verb:(create OR update OR patch) -@requestObject.spec.package:*sha256*
CLOUD
sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" objectRef.apiGroup="pkg.crossplane.io" (objectRef.resource="providers" OR objectRef.resource="configurations" OR objectRef.resource="functions") (verb="create" OR verb="update" OR verb="patch")
| rename requestObject.spec.package as package_ref, objectRef.name as object_name, objectRef.resource as kind, user.username as username
| where isnotnull(package_ref) AND NOT match(package_ref, "@sha256:")
| stats min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(username) as username, values(sourceIPs{}) as src_ips by package_ref, kind, object_name
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Crossplane ImageConfig signature-verification policy deleted or weakened AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on delete/update/patch operations against imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io in the Kubernetes audit stream. Crossplane enforces cosign signature verification only for images matched by an ImageConfig (spec.verification.cosign); removing or editing that resource silently disables verification, the defense the GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r TOCTOU already partially undermines. Surfaces whether the post-change object still carries a verification block. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's statement that 'package signature verification [is] configured via the ImageConfig mechanism' and Crossplane docs confirming the real resource (imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io, spec.verification.cosign). Detects the defense-evasion precursor — tearing down or weakening the cosign policy — using only verifiable API/resource names (no skipSignatureVerification field exists in the schema, so that reviewer suggestion was dropped as ungrounded). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r • https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/packages/image-configs/ • https://docs.upbound.io/providers/signature-verification
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Platform engineers legitimately rotating cosign authorities/keys inside an ImageConfig during key rollover
  • GitOps reconciliation re-applying an unchanged ImageConfig (server-side apply 'update' with no real diff)
  • Decommissioning an ImageConfig for a registry the org no longer uses
  • Migrating verification config between ImageConfig objects (delete old + create new)
  • Cert-manager or admission-controller status writes touching the resource
Suppression filter
| where Verb in ("delete", "deletecollection") or VerificationSpecPresent == false   // alert on removal/teardown of verification; suppress edits that retain a verification block
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the ImageConfig before/after the operation — confirm whether spec.verification.cosign authorities were removed, loosened, or the whole object deleted, and identify the actor (human vs service account) and source IP. A delete or removal of the verification block by a non-platform identity is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: restore the ImageConfig from source-of-truth/GitOps, and pause new package installs (or require digest pins) until verification is re-established; rotate credentials of the actor if unauthorized. 3) Hunt: list any package revisions installed while the ImageConfig was absent/weakened and check their Verified condition; cross-reference with the mutable-tag install detection to find packages that may have been pulled without enforced verification.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend ObjRef = todynamic(ObjectRef)
| where tostring(ObjRef.apiGroup) == "pkg.crossplane.io"
| where tostring(ObjRef.resource) == "imageconfigs"
| where Verb in ("delete", "deletecollection", "update", "patch")
| extend ReqObj = todynamic(RequestObject)
| extend VerificationSpecPresent = isnotempty(tostring(ReqObj.spec.verification))
| extend Actor = tostring(todynamic(User).username)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, Verb, ImageConfigName = tostring(ObjRef.name), UserAgent, VerificationSpecPresent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Crossplane ImageConfig Signature Verification Deleted Or Modified
id: b8f2d6a4-1c3e-4f7b-9a2d-6e4c8b1f0a52
description: Detects delete or modify operations against Crossplane ImageConfig resources, which configure cosign package signature verification. Removing or weakening an ImageConfig disables verification for matching package images (GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r).

  - https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/packages/image-configs/

    objectRef.apiGroup: 'pkg.crossplane.io'

level: medium

CLOUD
sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" objectRef.apiGroup="pkg.crossplane.io" objectRef.resource="imageconfigs" (verb="delete" OR verb="deletecollection" OR verb="update" OR verb="patch")

Anonymous HTTP 200 to DotVVM endpoints (AuthorizeActionFilter bypass exploitation) AIExploitation Low
Hunts successful (HTTP 200) requests to DotVVM-served content (.dothtml views / dotvvm resource routes) that carry no authenticated user, the observable signature of the no-op AuthorizeActionFilter letting unauthenticated callers reach pages it should have rejected with 401/403. Article-specific because it anchors on DotVVM's own request markers rather than a generic protected-path template. Rationale: Anchored on DotVVM's own request markers ('.dothtml', 'dotvvm' route) confirmed via dotvvm.com routing docs, combined with empty csUserName + scStatus 200 — the only behavioural signature the advisory leaves, since the no-op filter manifests as unauthenticated requests succeeding. defender_kql left empty: Microsoft Defender XDR has no IIS HTTP-status/authenticated-user table (DeviceNetworkEvents lacks HTTP status and request user). Cross-checked GitHub Advisory DB and GitLab advisory (CVSS 3.1, CWE-862). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/nuget/dotvvm/GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w/ • https://www.dotvvm.com/docs/2.0/pages/basics-routing
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Public, intentionally anonymous DotVVM pages (landing/login/marketing .dothtml views legitimately return 200 to anonymous users)
  • Static DotVVM resource handler fetches (CSS/JS bundled by the framework under dotvvm resource routes)
  • Load-balancer / uptime monitoring probes hitting DotVVM routes anonymously
  • Search-engine crawlers indexing public DotVVM content
  • Pre-auth bootstrap GET of a DotVVM SPA shell before the user signs in
Suppression filter
| where csMethod == "POST" or csUriStem !endswith ".css" and csUriStem !endswith ".js" and csUriStem !has "dotvvmResource"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target .dothtml route is meant to be protected (was it decorated with AuthorizeActionFilter?) and that the responding app runs a vulnerable DotVVM build (< 4.2.11, 4.3.0-preview01..4.3.14, or 5.0.0-preview01..08). If the page is public by design, close. 2) Contain: deploy the patched DotVVM (4.3.15 / 4.2.11 / 5.0.0-preview09) or swap AuthorizeActionFilter for AuthorizeAttribute per the advisory workaround; front the route with a WAF rule requiring a valid auth cookie. 3) Hunt: pull all anonymous-200 hits to this site for the same cIP set and review whether sensitive data (export/admin) was returned, then check app logs for state-changing POST postbacks executed without a principal.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where scStatus == 200
// DotVVM framework markers: .dothtml views or the dotvvm resource/postback route
| where csUriStem has "dotvvm" or csUriStem endswith ".dothtml" or csUriQuery has "dotvvm"
// no authenticated principal on the request = anonymous reach to a protected-by-design page
| where isempty(csUserName) or csUserName == "-"
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(csMethod, 10), Paths = make_set(csUriStem, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, cIP, sSiteName
| sort by Requests desc

Vulnerable DotVVM framework version present on host (GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w) AIExploitation Low
Exposure hunt that surfaces assets running a DotVVM build affected by the no-op AuthorizeActionFilter: any version < 4.2.11, the 4.3.x line below 4.3.15, or 5.0.0 previews 01-08. Concrete because it encodes the exact affected/patched version boundaries from the advisory. Rationale: Encodes the advisory's exact version boundaries — patched at 4.3.15 / 4.2.11 / 5.0.0-preview09 — with explicit handling of the preview-suffix branch so 5.0.0-preview08 is flagged but preview09 is not. Confidence Low because DotVVM is an embedded NuGet dependency and may not always appear in Defender TVM software inventory; where it does, the match is exact (fp low). Versions cross-checked against the GitHub and GitLab advisory entries. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/nuget/dotvvm/GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w/

Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DotVVM app that does not use AuthorizeActionFilter at all (vulnerable build present but feature unused — exposure, not exploitable)
  • Dev/test or internal-only hosts not reachable by untrusted users
  • A 4.3.15+ build whose installer string still carries a pre-release tag that parses to a lower core version
  • Side-by-side install where an old DotVVM copy lingers in a NuGet cache but the running app references the patched assembly
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged SoftwareVersion is the build actually loaded by a running, internet-reachable DotVVM app (not a stale cache copy), and that the app registers AuthorizeActionFilter. 2) Contain: schedule upgrade to 4.3.15 / 4.2.11 / 5.0.0-preview09 (or apply the AuthorizeAttribute workaround) on exposed hosts first. 3) Hunt: pivot each confirmed host into the anonymous-200 IIS hunt (companion UC) to see whether the no-op filter has already been exercised by unauthenticated callers.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "dotvvm" or SoftwareVendor has "dotvvm" or SoftwareVendor has "riganti"
| extend VerCore = extract(@"^(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion)
| where isnotempty(VerCore)
| extend V = parse_version(VerCore)
| extend PreviewNum = toint(extract(@"preview0*(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| where (V < parse_version("4.2.11"))                                                  // whole 4.2.x and earlier line
     or (V >= parse_version("4.3.0") and V < parse_version("4.3.15"))                   // 4.3.0-preview01..4.3.14
     or (V == parse_version("5.0.0") and SoftwareVersion has "preview" and PreviewNum < 9) // 5.0.0-preview01..08
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| sort by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SoftwareName has "dotvvm" or SoftwareVendor has "dotvvm" or SoftwareVendor has "riganti"
| extend VerCore = extract(@"^(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion)
| where isnotempty(VerCore)
| extend V = parse_version(VerCore)
| extend PreviewNum = toint(extract(@"preview0*(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| where (V < parse_version("4.2.11"))
     or (V >= parse_version("4.3.0") and V < parse_version("4.3.15"))
     or (V == parse_version("5.0.0") and SoftwareVersion has "preview" and PreviewNum < 9)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| sort by DeviceName asc

Network-AI sandbox escape: node spawns /bin/sh -c with allowlist prefix + shell metacharacter injection AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-54051 core exploit: the network-ai SandboxPolicy allowlist glob-matches the whole command string but ShellExecutor runs it via /bin/sh -c, so an allowed prefix (git/npm/node/yarn/pnpm) followed by ;, &&, ||, $() or backticks becomes arbitrary execution. Surfaces a node parent spawning a shell with -c where the command line carries both an allowlisted prefix and an unquoted shell metacharacter. Rationale: Uses the exact mechanism named in the article — node/npm/git/yarn/pnpm allowlist prefixes glob-matched whole-string, executed through /bin/sh -c, plus the article's enumerated metacharacter set (; & | $ ` ( ) < > { }). The node-parent + sh -c + prefix + metachar combination is the article's primary exploit (UC_12_2).
ATT&CKT1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm lifecycle scripts that chain shell commands with && (e.g. "build && test")
  • CI/CD runners (Jenkins, GitLab runner) invoking node tooling that shells out
  • pm2 / nodemon process managers launching shell wrappers
  • Developer running a node script that calls git with a $(...) subshell
  • Postinstall hooks combining multiple commands with ;
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run","npm exec","yarn run","node_modules/.bin") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("&&","||") and not ProcessCommandLine has_any ("id;","whoami","/tmp/","curl ","wget ","nc "))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent node command line; identify whether the shell payload follows a legitimate allowlist prefix and whether the metacharacter introduces an unrelated command (id, curl, nc) vs a benign build chain. 2) Contain: if the host runs network-ai < 5.9.1 and the injected segment is non-build (recon/network), isolate the host and kill the orchestrator process; capture /proc and any dropped marker files. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same node parent for child recon binaries and outbound connections; check for network-ai version and remove broad wildcard allowlist entries (node */npm *).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-c"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\b(git|npm|node|yarn|pnpm)\b"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"[;&|`$(){}<>]"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-c"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\b(git|npm|node|yarn|pnpm)\b"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"[;&|`$(){}<>]"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network-AI CVE-2026-54051 post-exploit: Linux recon utilities spawned from shell child of node AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the post-exploitation enumeration that follows a successful CVE-2026-54051 allowlist bypass: a shell (sh/bash/dash) whose parent is node executing reconnaissance binaries. Fires when the orchestrator-spawned shell runs id, whoami, uname, hostname, curl, wget, nc, ncat, python, perl, ssh-keygen or cat. Rationale: Maps the article's post-exploitation profile (id ran via the injected /bin/sh -c in the PoC) and the reviewer-supplied recon binary set, scoped to a node grandparent in Defender/Falcon where InitiatingProcessParentFileName is available. Sentinel ImProcessCreate exposes only parent (sh) so the node grandparent constraint is relaxed there.
ATT&CKT1033 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based deploy scripts legitimately calling curl/wget to fetch artifacts
  • Healthcheck wrappers running id/whoami/hostname inside containers
  • CI jobs invoking python via a shell step
  • Admin troubleshooting scripts under a node-managed service
  • Container entrypoint shells gathering uname/hostname at startup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/healthcheck","/entrypoint","deploy.sh") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the grandparent is the network-ai orchestrator node process and the recon command was not part of a known deploy/healthcheck script; review the preceding sh -c command line for an injected metacharacter. 2) Contain: if recon is paired with outbound nc/curl/wget to an untrusted host, isolate the device and snapshot the process tree and any written files. 3) Hunt: search the same host/account for the allowlist-bypass parent event (UC1), outbound C2, ssh-keygen output, and credential file reads; verify network-ai is upgraded to >= 5.9.1.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "node"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","ssh-keygen","cat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","ssh-keygen","cat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network-AI CVE-2026-54051 proof-of-concept artifact execution (poc-316.js / PWNED-316.txt) AIExploitation High
Hunts for execution or file activity referencing the published CVE-2026-54051 PoC artifacts — the poc-316.js exploit script and its PWNED-316.txt success marker. A direct, high-fidelity indicator of active testing or exploitation of the network-ai allowlist bypass. Rationale: Targets the literal exploit artifacts named in the article PoC (`node poc-316.js`, marker `PWNED-316.txt`). These strings are unique to CVE-2026-54051 testing, giving a very low-FP alerting signal across process and file telemetry.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally validating the patch by running the published PoC
  • A vulnerability scanner or red-team toolkit shipping poc-316.js
  • A file named poc-316.js committed to an internal research repo and opened by an editor
  • Mirror/backup process copying a saved copy of the advisory PoC
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host belongs to an authorised security/red-team tester; check the parent process (node) and whether PWNED-316.txt was actually written. 2) Contain: on a non-authorised host, isolate it, preserve poc-316.js and any marker file, and kill the network-ai orchestrator process. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1/UC2 on the same host/account for the allowlist-bypass parent and post-exploit recon; confirm network-ai is upgraded to >= 5.9.1 and remove wildcard allowlist entries.

Vulnerable network-ai (<=5.7.1) npm package present in node_modules AIDelivery High
Asset-inventory hunt that surfaces hosts with the vulnerable Jovancoding/Network-AI package on disk (CVE-2026-48814 / CVE-2026-46701). The package files land under node_modules\network-ai; presence is the precondition for the unauthenticated MCP SSE exposure. Triage version against the 5.7.2 fixed release. Rationale: Pivots on the concrete install path 'node_modules\network-ai' named in the advisory (bin/mcp-server.ts, lib/mcp-transport-sse.ts live under it). Cache-path exclusions cut npm/pnpm store noise so only real project installs surface for remediation against the 5.7.2 fix. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/network-ai/CVE-2026-46701/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-48814-cwe-306-missing-authentication-for--a37c283f4afc7554 • https://www.squaredtech.co/mcp-security-flaw-npm-package-ships-with-no-auth-by-default

network-ai MCP SSE server launched in non-stdio (vulnerable) mode AIInstallation High
Detects process creation of the Network-AI MCP server (command line contains both 'network-ai' and 'mcp-server') without the --stdio flag, i.e. the SSE listener that ships with the empty-default-secret authorization bypass. Stdio-mode invocations are excluded because the advisory's only safe path requires --stdio. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact invocation tokens — the 'network-ai' package and its 'mcp-server' bin — and excludes --stdio, the only mode the advisory deems non-vulnerable. Surfaces the listening SSE server before exploitation rather than a generic node process. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/network-ai/CVE-2026-46701/ • https://www.squaredtech.co/mcp-security-flaw-npm-package-ships-with-no-auth-by-default

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator running the server locally bound to 127.0.0.1 for legitimate single-user use
  • Developer testing network-ai during feature work
  • Automated integration-test harness spinning the server up and tearing it down
  • Patched 5.7.2+ host where the secret is now enforced (still launches the same process — confirm version)
  • Container entrypoint launching the SSE server with a properly set NETWORK_AI_MCP_SECRET
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the on-disk network-ai version (<=5.7.1 = exposed) and whether NETWORK_AI_MCP_SECRET is set in the service/unit/container env; an empty/unset secret means _isAuthorized() returns true for all callers. 2) Contain: stop the SSE listener or rebind it to loopback, set a strong NETWORK_AI_MCP_SECRET, and upgrade to 5.7.2+. 3) Hunt: pull DeviceNetworkEvents/web logs for this host and run the inbound-POST /mcp UC to see whether any non-loopback caller already reached config_set / agent_spawn / token_* tools.

Unauthenticated non-loopback POST /mcp tool invocation against network-ai SSE server AIExploitation Medium
Active-exploitation detection for CVE-2026-48814: a non-loopback caller (curl/SSRF/0.0.0.0 bind) issues POST /mcp to the Network-AI SSE server and gets HTTP 200 with no Authorization header, invoking MCP tools (config_set, agent_spawn, blackboard_write, token_*) against the empty default secret. Web/proxy logs carry the path+method+auth-header signal; EDR network telemetry carries the non-loopback inbound exposure. Rationale: Targets the advisory's PoC exactly — POST /mcp, HTTP 200, no auth, non-loopback source — using the web-log auth-header emptiness (ImWebSession.HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) as the unauthenticated signal, with EDR inbound-non-loopback as a corroborating exposure pivot when proxy logs are absent. Datadog left blank: no generic web-access-log source in this tenant's listed schema carries POST/path/auth-header. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/network-ai/CVE-2026-46701/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-48814-cwe-306-missing-authentication-for--a37c283f4afc7554 • https://www.squaredtech.co/mcp-security-flaw-npm-package-ships-with-no-auth-by-default
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner / ASM probing the /mcp endpoint
  • Authorized local MCP client legitimately sending no Authorization header because the secret was never configured (still the vuln — worth flagging)
  • Reverse-proxy or container health check polling /mcp
  • Container/NAT bridge rewriting a loopback request so it appears as a non-loopback SrcIpAddr
  • Load balancer or service mesh sidecar fronting the SSE server with stripped auth headers
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination host runs network-ai <=5.7.1 SSE mode, then inspect the request URL/body for invoked tool names (config_set, agent_spawn, blackboard_write, token_revoke) and check the source IP against known scanners and internal ranges. 2) Contain: block ingress to the MCP port from non-loopback sources at the host/SG firewall, set a strong NETWORK_AI_MCP_SECRET, restart the service, and upgrade to 5.7.2+. 3) Hunt: enumerate every POST /mcp 200 from this source across all hosts, review token_* and config_set invocations for tampering or stolen credentials, and rotate any tokens the blackboard/agent tools could have exposed.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "network-ai" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "mcp-server"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--stdio"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType != "Loopback" and RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Ports=make_set(LocalPort, 10) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/mcp"
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

gemini-mcp-tool @file path-traversal / sensitive-file exfiltration via Gemini CLI AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Gemini CLI invocations (driven by the gemini-mcp-tool MCP server, CVE-2026-0755) whose command line carries an @file reference that escapes the working directory or targets sensitive files (@/etc/passwd, @~/.ssh/id_rsa, @../../secret). Article-specific because it keys on the Gemini CLI @file parser abuse used to read/exfiltrate arbitrary local files through the LLM channel. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact @file PoC strings (@/etc/passwd, @~/.ssh/id_rsa, @../../secret) scoped to a 'gemini' command line — the CVE-2026-0755 exfiltration sink. Cross-checked against the GitLab Advisory DB and Snyk entries which confirm the @file parser as the read/exfil vector. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/gemini-mcp-tool/CVE-2026-0755/ • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-GEMINIMCPTOOL-15091895 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-0755/

  • Security researcher reproducing the CVE in an authorized test lab

Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)@\.\./[A-Za-z0-9._-]+/(src|lib|test|tests|docs)/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent (expect node.exe running the gemini-mcp-tool MCP server). Confirm the @file target is outside the project working directory and is sensitive (passwd, id_rsa, .env, cloud creds). Identify who/what supplied the prompt (MCP client, chat session, automated agent). 2) Contain: kill the MCP server process, upgrade gemini-mcp-tool to >=1.1.6, and rotate any credential file referenced (SSH keys, tokens) since the content was sent to the Gemini API. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to the Gemini API from this host around the event, search other hosts for the same gemini @traversal pattern, and check the MCP client logs for the originating untrusted prompt.
